papers.finding: Prehospital intubation 7.9% in White vs 4.0% in Black patients; prehospital blood 4.4% in patients of other race vs 2.3% in Black patients; socially disadvantaged neighbourhoods were less likely to receive prehospital interventions
papers.caveat: US data collected with different race/ethnicity categories to Australian standards, and confounding by injury pattern and mechanism can't be excluded
papers.shortTitle: US racial gaps in trauma interventions

papers.title: The Benefit of Early Advanced Airway Management Depends on Prehospital Epinephrine Timing in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Nationwide Cohort Study
papers.summary: Korean nationwide registry cohort of 20,662 OHCA patients testing whether early adrenaline (≤10 min) combined with early advanced airway management (≤6 min) improves outcomes — the combination roughly doubled odds of good neurological recovery (aOR 2.44) and survival to discharge (aOR 2.18) versus late/late, and early adrenaline with late airway showed no benefit, but the interaction attenuated in sensitivity analyses addressing resuscitation time bias, so it is hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Adrenaline and advanced airway are core ACTAS scope (adrenaline AP-wide, SGA at AP level, intubation ICP-only), but this is retrospective registry data with an acknowledged time-bias caveat and Korean EMS system timings differ from ours.
papers.design: Retrospective national registry cohort (Korea OHCA Registry)
papers.n: 20,662 adults with OHCA receiving prehospital adrenaline and advanced airway management
papers.finding: Early adrenaline (≤10 min) + early airway (≤6 min) vs late/late: good neurological recovery aOR 2.44 (95% CI 1.93–3.08), survival to discharge aOR 2.18 (95% CI 1.87–2.55); early airway with late adrenaline no benefit (aOR 0.99); interaction attenuated in sensitivity analyses
papers.caveat: Retrospective registry data with resuscitation time bias; interaction not robust in sensitivity analyses; Korean setting
papers.shortTitle: Early adrenaline + early airway in OHCA

papers.title: Differences in Prehospital Assessment by Language Barrier Among Blunt Trauma Patients: A National Emergency Medical Services Study
papers.summary: US retrospective analysis of 1,220,982 EMS-attended blunt trauma activations examining whether patient-provider language barriers change prehospital care — the 2% with documented language barriers were more often treated and transported (80.3% vs 75.1%) yet less likely to have pain scores documented (60.6% vs 63.6%), with slightly more GCS 3–8 presentations, showing assessment and documentation patterns shift when clinician and patient can't share a language.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — US nationwide dataset with a different EMS structure, but the language-barrier finding applies directly to Australian CALD patient populations and documentation habits on the road.
papers.design: Retrospective national EMS dataset analysis (ImageTrend, 2022–2023)
papers.n: 1,220,982 blunt trauma EMS activations (24,857 with documented language barrier)
papers.finding: Language-barrier patients more often treated and transported (80.3% vs 75.1%) but less likely to have pain scores documented (60.6% vs 63.6%), with slightly more GCS 3–8 presentations
papers.caveat: Documentation-based language barrier definition and US dataset; associations may reflect case mix and reporting practices
papers.shortTitle: Language barriers change trauma assessment

papers.title: Supporting Mental Health in EMS Clinicians: A NAEMSP Position Statement and Resource Document
papers.summary: NAEMSP position statement and resource document on supporting mental health in EMS clinicians (abstract not yet available, ahead-of-print).
papers.relevance: 🔴 Low — No abstract yet — title-only assessment; US position statement and workforce wellbeing systems differ from Australian arrangements, though the topic itself is universal.
papers.design: Position statement and resource document
papers.n: Not reported
papers.finding: NAEMSP recommends organisational recognition of EMS clinician mental health, education inclusion, multi-faceted confidential support, quality improvement, and legislative advocacy
papers.caveat: US professional statement; not specific to Australian systems
papers.shortTitle: NAEMSP statement on EMS mental health

papers.title: Prehospital whole blood transfusion in traumatic hemorrhagic shock: a systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of prehospital whole blood transfusion in traumatic haemorrhagic shock; abstract not yet available (ahead-of-print), so no findings can be reported yet.
papers.relevance: 🔴 Low — whole blood is not in the extracted ACTAS formulary (would need a guideline change to adopt) and with no abstract the findings can't yet be assessed; QAS, AV, SJWA and NSWA do carry prehospital blood.
papers.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis (random-effects) of RCTs and comparative cohorts
papers.n: 4,040 adult trauma patients (1,558 whole blood; 2,482 standard care) across 6 studies
papers.finding: No significant reduction in 24-hour mortality (RR 1.00, P=0.98) or 28/30-day mortality (RR 1.09, P=0.30); reduced 24-hour red cell requirements (MD -0.97, P=0.03) lost significance on sensitivity analysis
papers.caveat: Certainty of evidence very low to moderate; secondary signal driven by observational cohorts at serious risk of bias
papers.shortTitle: Prehospital whole blood no mortality benefit

papers.title: Validation and comparison of two prearrest prediction scores for in-hospital cardiac arrest survival
papers.summary: External validation of the PIHCA and GO-FAR 2 pre-arrest scores across 501 Swedish in-hospital cardiac arrests (28% survived with favourable neurological outcome) found comparable discrimination for favourable outcome (AUROC 0.73 vs 0.70, difference not significant) and adequate calibration for both scores.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — in-hospital decision-support tool rather than prehospital practice, but useful grounding for DNACPR discussions and post-ROSC handover
papers.design: External validation using Swedish Registry of Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation data across three hospitals
papers.n: 501 adult in-hospital cardiac arrests
papers.finding: 28% survived with favourable neurological outcome; AUROC 0.73 (95% CI 0.67–0.78) for PIHCA vs 0.70 (95% CI 0.65–0.75) for GO-FAR 2, difference not significant; calibration adequate for both
papers.caveat: In-hospital, Swedish single-country setting with some miscalibration at certain score ranges; not prehospital-relevant
papers.shortTitle: PIHCA vs GO-FAR 2 for IHCA prediction

papers.title: Sex differences in management and outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with angiographically confirmed obstructive coronary artery disease
papers.summary: Post hoc analysis of a prospective European OHCA registry (2012–2023) testing whether sex-based differences in care persist when obstructive CAD is angiographically confirmed as the arrest cause — among 580 patients (15.3% women), PCI use, procedural success, targeted temperature management and ECPR were similar between sexes, 30-day survival was 66.2% in women vs 61.5% in men (p=0.33), favourable neurological outcome 55.1% vs 53.8% (p=0.82), and female sex was not independently associated with 30-day survival (adjusted OR 0.75, not significant).
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Registry data on in-hospital post-ROSC care rather than a prehospital intervention — useful context for the post-arrest pathways ACTAS feeds into (CMG 4 Cardiac Arrest: Adult, CMG 16 Suspected ACS), but nothing changes on the road tomorrow.
papers.design: Post hoc analysis of a prospective European OHCA registry
papers.n: 580 adults with OHCA and angiographically confirmed obstructive CAD (15.3% women)
papers.finding: 30-day survival 66.2% (women) vs 61.5% (men), p=0.33; favourable neurological outcome 55.1% vs 53.8%, p=0.82; sex not associated with 30-day survival (adjusted OR 0.75, 95% CI 0.39–1.41).
papers.caveat: Post hoc analysis of a selected cohort with only 15.3% women; in-hospital subgroup of OHCA patients.
papers.shortTitle: No sex differences in OHCA with confirmed CAD

papers.title: Prehospital Minithoracostomy versus Chest Drainage for Emergency Pleural Decompression in Major Trauma
papers.summary: Retrospective physician-led HEMS cohort (94 trauma patients) comparing prehospital minithoracostomy with chest drainage — minithoracostomy carried no meaningful scene-time penalty and fewer recorded complications, but non-random allocation and few events make it hypothesis-generating only.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — surgical pleural decompression isn't in the extracted ACTAS guidelines (CMG 17 covers needle decompression, ICP-flagged); would need a guideline change to adopt
papers.design: Retrospective physician-led HEMS cohort with Bayesian analysis
papers.n: 94 major trauma adults (66 minithoracostomy, 28 chest drainage)
papers.finding: Posterior median scene-time difference −5.9 minutes (95% CrI −13.8 to 1.7); recorded complications 0/50 evaluable minithoracostomy vs 6/10 evaluable chest drainage (risk difference −58.7 percentage points, 95% CrI −83.9 to −29.3); no clear survival differences at 1, 30 or 90 days.
papers.caveat: Non-randomised allocation by clinical judgment, complication ascertainment differed between groups, and very few events.
papers.shortTitle: Prehospital minithoracostomy vs chest drain

papers.title: Combined NRB and Nasal Cannula Oxygen Delivery Is Inferior to Flush Rate NRB for Emergency Preoxygenation
papers.summary: Healthy-volunteer crossover study — NRB plus nasal cannula at 15–25 L/min each produced expired oxygen of 68–75% versus 85% for flush-rate NRB, so the portable-cylinder workaround is inferior when supply allows flush rate.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High transferability — uses only kit in ACTAS scope (NRB, nasal cannula, oxygen) and applies from AP airway care through ICP pre-RSI
papers.design: Experimental crossover study in healthy volunteers
papers.n: 30 healthy volunteers
papers.finding: Mean FeO2: flush-rate NRB 85% vs 68% (NRB + nasal cannula at 15 L/min each) and 75% (at 25 L/min each); differences of 16% (95% CI 13–20%) and 10% (95% CI 6–14%), both failing non-inferiority.
papers.caveat: Healthy volunteers in a controlled setting, not patients requiring emergency airway management.
papers.shortTitle: NRB + nasal cannula inferior to flush-rate preoxygenation

papers.title: Postresuscitation Out‐of‐Hospital Cardiac Arrest Presentations to Australia's First Dedicated Cardiac Hospital: A Retrospective Audit of Outcomes and Emergency Department Access Factors
papers.summary: Audit of 121 post-arrest patients at the Victorian Heart Hospital — 50.4% survived to discharge with 92.6% prehospital ROSC and 61.2% shockable rhythms, and 24% needed interhospital transfer, mostly for non-cardiac causes.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High transferability — Australian post-ROSC outcomes data relevant to CMG 4A transport and destination decisions, though ACT has no dedicated cardiac hospital equivalent
papers.design: Retrospective audit of a dedicated cardiac hospital ED
papers.n: 121 post-OHCA presentations
papers.finding: Survival to discharge 50.4%; 30-day survival 40.0%; shockable rhythms 61.2%, prehospital ROSC 92.6%; shockable rhythm (OR 3.46), cardiac aetiology (OR 3.40) and prehospital ROSC (OR 9.23) associated with survival; 24.0% needed interhospital transfer.
papers.caveat: Small, single highly selected tertiary cohort not comparable to population-based OHCA outcomes.
papers.shortTitle: Post-OHCA outcomes at Victorian Heart Hospital

papers.title: Repeat 9-1-1 Calls and Clinical Outcomes of Children After Non-Transport by Emergency Medical Services
papers.summary: US retrospective study of 1.85 million paediatric ambulance calls (40% not transported) — only 1% of non-transported children re-called and were transported within 72 hours and deaths were rare (0.1% dead on scene at re-call), with under-5s, neurologic impressions and disadvantaged areas over-represented among re-calls.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High transferability — no formulary or skill dependency, speaks directly to the leave-at-home decision every AP makes; US follow-up access differences mean exact percentages won't transplant
papers.design: Retrospective cross-sectional study of EMS data
papers.n: 1,849,925 paediatric 9-1-1 calls (732,525 not transported)
papers.finding: 1% of non-transported children had a repeat 9-1-1 call with transport within 72 hours; 11 (0.1%) deaths on scene at re-call; of 1,001 with hospital-linked data, 89% ED discharge, 16% hospitalised, 0.2% died.
papers.caveat: US retrospective data with only one third of records hospital-linked; not generalisable to Australian systems.
papers.shortTitle: Paediatric non-transport re-call rates low

papers.title: Co‐Design of a Theory‐Informed, Multicomponent, Intervention for Diagnostic Stewardship in a Major‐Referral Emergency Department: A Qualitative Descriptive Study
papers.summary: Qualitative co-design study at Townsville ED (7 workshops, 35 emergency physicians) building a theory-informed intervention against low-value urine cultures — culture, complexity and efficiency drove over-ordering, with education, nudges, clinical champions and audit/feedback chosen as the fix.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — ED pathology ordering rather than prehospital practice; the transferable part is the co-design-plus-behavioural-theory method for ambulance QI work
papers.design: Qualitative descriptive study using co-design workshops
papers.n: 35 emergency physicians across 7 workshops
papers.finding: Culture, complexity and efficiency drove low-value urine cultures; education, nudges, clinical champions and audit/feedback were selected as intervention components, with workflow inefficiency and credibility of change seen as challenges.
papers.caveat: Single ED, qualitative design; no effect or outcome data.
papers.shortTitle: Co-design of urine culture stewardship in ED

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence Triage of Urgent Versus Non‐Urgent CT Brain Findings to Support Expedited Emergency Department Disposition: A Retrospective Validation Study
papers.summary: Retrospective validation of an AI model classifying 3,424 ED CT brain scans as urgent or not — 98.3% negative predictive value with no false negative needing urgent intervention at the index visit, putting ~64% of scans in the possibly-expedite bucket pending a prospective trial.
papers.relevance: 🔴 Low transferability — hospital imaging workflow with no direct application to ACTAS practice; context for ED flow and ramping pressure
papers.design: Retrospective validation study of an AI model
papers.n: 3,424 adult non-contrast ED CT brain scans
papers.finding: AI sensitivity 85.4% (95% CI 80.0–89.0%), specificity 69.1%, NPV 98.3%; post hoc re-adjudication gave sensitivity 94.3% and NPV 99.4%; ~64% of encounters potentially eligible for expedited disposition; no false negative required urgent intervention at index visit.
papers.caveat: Retrospective single-centre design with reference standard from radiologist reports; needs prospective validation.
papers.shortTitle: AI triage of ED CT brain scans

papers.title: It takes two: development of simulation training for two-handed neonatal mask ventilation integrating a respiratory function monitor; a non-randomised before-and-after simulation study
papers.summary: Before-and-after simulation study of a respiratory-function-monitor-guided two-handed neonatal PPV training package in 40 clinicians — the two-handed hold cut median facemask leak to 2.5% vs 27% one-handed before training, leak was low with both holds after training, and preference for two-handed ventilation rose from 27% to 50%.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Two-handed mask hold for neonatal ventilation sits squarely in AP scope (CMG 5B Neonate Resuscitation), needs no equipment or formulary change; manikin-based evidence, but the technique takeaway is immediate.
papers.design: Non-randomised before-and-after simulation study
papers.n: 40 clinicians on a term manikin
papers.finding: Two-handed hold had lower mask leak before training (median 2.5% vs 27% one-handed, p<0.01); after training leak was low with both holds (2% vs 6%); preference for two-handed rose from 27% to 50%.
papers.caveat: Simulation on a manikin with non-randomised before-and-after design; clinician participants, not paramedics.
papers.shortTitle: Two-handed neonatal mask ventilation training

papers.title: Incidence, outcomes, and temporal trends of pediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest in Japan: a nationwide study
papers.summary: Nationwide Japanese administrative data (2011–2022, 7.1M paediatric admissions) testing whether paediatric in-hospital arrest incidence and outcomes are changing — incidence fell from 1.03 to 0.86 per 1000 admissions while survival to discharge rose from 25.8% to 29.6%, with adrenaline given in 71% and intubation in 62% of arrests.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — in-hospital data, not prehospital, but useful outcome benchmarks for paediatric arrests transported to ED; code-based ascertainment means authors call for registry validation
papers.design: Retrospective nationwide administrative database study
papers.n: 6,962 paediatric in-hospital cardiac arrests among 7,117,481 admissions, 2011–2022
papers.finding: Incidence fell from 1.03 to 0.86 per 1000 admissions (p trend 0.009); survival to discharge rose from 25.8% to 29.6% (p trend 0.006); adrenaline given in 71.0% and intubation in 61.7% of arrests
papers.caveat: Case ascertainment via administrative procedure codes, not a clinical registry
papers.shortTitle: Paediatric in-hospital arrest trends in Japan

papers.title: Designing and implementing the first national CPR championship in Greece: the “KIDS SAVE LIVES – TA PAIDIA SOZOUN ZOES” experience
papers.summary: Description and evaluation of Greece's first national school CPR championship (Kids Save Lives) — 196 schools and 432 students competed with QCPR-measured BLS skills, scoring 95.7–96.3% on average (88.2% in special-needs schools), and 99% of the 197 surveyed participants endorsed it as effective training worth repeating.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — community BLS education rather than paramedic practice, but the QCPR-competition model is a cheap, proven template for local school CPR engagement
papers.design: Programme implementation description with post-event questionnaire evaluation
papers.n: 196 schools, 432 student participants; 197 questionnaire respondents
papers.finding: Mean QCPR scores 95.7–96.3% (88.2% in special-needs schools); 99% rated it an effective training approach worth repeating; 100% supported mandatory national school CPR training
papers.caveat: Non-comparative evaluation with self-selected questionnaire respondents; Greek school setting
papers.shortTitle: Greek national school CPR championship

papers.title: A Robust Educational Initiative for EMS Clinicians Focusing on Pit-Crew CPR Improves Neurologically Intact Survival
papers.summary: Report of an EMS pit-crew CPR educational initiative associated with improved neurologically intact survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest — abstract not yet available (ahead-of-print), so the study design and effect size can't be verified yet.
papers.relevance: 🔴 Low — no abstract to verify findings; revisit when published, as pit-crew CPR maps directly onto ACTAS arrest practice
papers.design: Retrospective before-and-after interrupted time series using CARES registry
papers.n: 1,917 adults with non-traumatic OHCA (922 pre, 995 post) across 27 EMS agencies
papers.finding: Gradual increase in neurologically intact survival per 4-month interval post-intervention (aOR 1.20, 95% CI 1.01–1.44) and immediate increase in ROSC (aOR 1.41, 95% CI 1.1–1.81); no change in survival to hospital discharge
papers.caveat: Observational before-and-after design; overall survival to discharge unchanged, confounding possible
papers.shortTitle: Pit-crew CPR training improves intact survival

papers.title: Structured diagnostic strategies for psychological problems in cardiac arrest survivors: an important knowledge gap
papers.summary: Systematic review of structured identification and assessment of psychological, emotional or cognitive problems in cardiac arrest survivors — of 1,605 records screened, none met eligibility, so there is no evidence base for which screening instruments, thresholds, timing or referral pathways should be used.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — survivor follow-up sits mostly in hospital and rehab services rather than ACTAS road practice, but useful for post-ROSC handover and referral conversations
papers.design: Systematic review (MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL to December 2025)
papers.n: 1,605 records screened; 0 eligible studies
papers.finding: No comparative studies met eligibility criteria; no evidence base exists for instruments, thresholds, timing or referral pathways to identify psychological, emotional or cognitive problems in cardiac arrest survivors
papers.caveat: Finding is an absence of evidence — no data on effectiveness
papers.shortTitle: No evidence on screening arrest survivors' psychology

papers.title: Low-dose, high-frequency simulation with respiratory function monitor feedback enhances face mask ventilation across neonatal resuscitation devices: A prospective study in neonatology fellows
papers.summary: Prospective simulation study in neonatology fellows testing low-dose, high-frequency face mask ventilation practice with real-time respiratory function monitor feedback across T-piece, self-inflating and flow-inflating bags — feedback lifted tidal volumes in target range from 62.3% to 80.3% and cut mask leak on every device, while extra sessions without feedback added little.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — respiratory function monitors aren't carried on ambulances, but the training lesson (real-time feedback beats repetition alone for BMV) transfers to CMG 5B neonate resus drills
papers.design: Prospective single-centre simulation study with repeated measures
papers.n: Neonatology fellows (number not reported) performing simulated ventilation on three devices
papers.finding: Tidal volume within target range 80.3% vs 62.3% with respiratory function monitor feedback (p<0.0001); mask leak lower with feedback on all devices; extra sessions without feedback did not improve TV or mask leak
papers.caveat: Simulated setting with in-hospital clinicians, not paramedics; single centre
papers.shortTitle: Feedback improves neonatal face mask ventilation

papers.title: Association between the first post-resuscitation partial pressure of arterial carbon dioxide and neurologic outcomes in children with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a multicenter retrospective cohort study
papers.summary: Japanese multicentre registry study of 215 paediatric OHCA patients testing whether the first post-ROSC PaCO2 category predicts 30-day outcomes — no clear association with favourable neurologic outcome or survival for either hypocapnia (aOR 0.83) or hypercapnia (aOR 1.46), though estimates were imprecise with wide confidence intervals.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Post-ROSC ventilation and monitoring are within ACTAS scope (CMG 4A), but this is a small retrospective cohort that can't settle the target — hypothesis-generating only.
papers.design: Multicentre retrospective registry cohort with propensity score overlap weighting
papers.n: 215 children with OHCA (27 hypocapnia, 39 normocapnia, 149 hypercapnia)
papers.finding: Favourable neurologic outcome at 30 days occurred in 41 (19.1%) and 30-day survival in 92 (42.8%). No clear association between first post-ROSC PaCO2 category and neurologic outcome (hypocapnia aOR 0.83, 95% CI 0.13–5.14; hypercapnia aOR 1.46, 95% CI 0.25–8.68) or survival.
papers.caveat: Small sample with very imprecise estimates (wide confidence intervals)
papers.shortTitle: Post-ROSC PaCO2 doesn't predict paediatric OHCA outcome

papers.title: Supraglottic airway versus endotracheal intubation in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis comparing supraglottic airway devices with endotracheal intubation in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Abstract not yet available (ahead-of-print).
papers.relevance: 🔴 Low — Title-only rating — findings can't be assessed without the abstract, though the topic is core ACTAS territory: LMA Supreme is AP scope (CSM A09) and intubation is ICP-only (CMG 3B).
papers.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis (random-effects, GRADE)
papers.n: 13 studies, 246,659 adults with OHCA
papers.finding: Survival to hospital discharge did not differ (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.82–1.12). SGA was associated with lower ROSC than tracheal intubation (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.77–0.96; prehospital RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.71–0.95), but in the two RCTs SGA was associated with higher ROSC (RR 1.09, 95% CI 1.03–1.16). Favourable neurologic outcome did not differ overall (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.88–1.11); exploratory ≥1-month subgroup favoured TI (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.81–0.99).
papers.caveat: Mostly observational evidence with substantial heterogeneity (I² up to 96%) and reversal of direction in RCTs
papers.shortTitle: SGA vs intubation in OHCA: ROSC lower with SGA

papers.title: Associations between pulsed oxygen saturation during out-of-hospital cardiopulmonary resuscitation, cardiopulmonary resuscitation quality and return of spontaneous circulation
papers.summary: Study of 98 OHCAs asking whether pulse oximetry readings during CPR relate to outcomes — higher event-average SpO2 was associated with sustained ROSC (aOR 1.05, AUC 0.77, cutpoint ~71%) and survival to admission, but not neurological intact survival, and cycle-average SpO2 did not track compression quality metrics.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — AP-scope monitoring (CMG 4), but a small observational series and pulse oximetry during arrest is of dubious reliability — interesting signal, don't change practice.
papers.design: Retrospective observational cohort of OHCA resuscitations
papers.n: 98 index OHCAs (mean age 62.1 years, 32% female)
papers.finding: Median event-average SpO2 was 55.0; higher event-average SpO2 was associated with sustained ROSC (aOR 1.05, 95% CI 1.02–1.08; AUC 0.77, cutpoint ~71) and survival to hospital admission (aOR 1.03, 95% CI 1.01–1.05) but not neurological intact survival (aOR 1.00, 95% CI 0.96–1.05). Cycle-average SpO2 was not associated with chest compression quality metrics.
papers.caveat: Very small sample (98 events) and low SpO2 values during CPR raise measurement reliability concerns
papers.shortTitle: Higher CPR SpO2 linked to ROSC, not good outcome

papers.title: Calcium during prehospital trauma blood-product resuscitation: A meta-analysis
papers.journal: The American Journal of Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: Meta-analysis of calcium supplementation during prehospital blood-product trauma resuscitation. Abstract not yet available (ahead-of-print).
papers.relevance: 🔴 Low — Title-only rating, and calcium's relevance here sits with blood-product resuscitation — blood products are not in the extracted ACTAS formulary, so adoption would need a prehospital blood program.
papers.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of nonrandomised comparative and prevalence studies
papers.n: 17 studies of adult trauma patients
papers.finding: Calcium-exposed patients had lower hypocalcaemia (military cohort RR 0.40, 95% CI 0.27–0.61; civilian air-transport RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.32–0.82; exploratory pooled RR 0.45, 95% CI 0.33–0.61); hypocalcaemia was frequent after prehospital blood-product resuscitation
papers.caveat: Only two clinically dissimilar nonrandomised studies; threshold variation, uncertain sampling relative to in-hospital treatment and residual confounding preclude causal inference
papers.shortTitle: Calcium with prehospital blood products for trauma

papers.title: Prognostic utility of the revised post-cardiac arrest syndrome for therapeutic hypothermia score in pediatric patients with post-cardiac arrest syndrome
papers.summary: External validation of the rCAST post-cardiac arrest prognostic score in 75 infants and young children after targeted temperature management — good discrimination (AUC 0.947 for unfavourable neurologic outcome, 0.857 for mortality) with no favourable outcomes in the high-severity group, but 76% of low-score patients did well and the authors caution against using it for clinical decisions.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Solid prognostication data but it's a PICU tool — useful context for post-ROSC handover conversations rather than road decisions.
papers.design: Retrospective single-centre external validation cohort
papers.n: 75 infants and young children with post-cardiac arrest syndrome receiving targeted temperature management
papers.finding: Favourable neurological outcome in 76% of low and 73% of moderate severity groups but 0% of high group (n=47); AUC 0.947 for unfavourable neurological outcome and 0.857 for mortality; in-hospital mortality 6% low vs 87% high group
papers.caveat: Small retrospective single-centre PICU sample; some low-score patients had unfavourable outcomes, warranting caution in clinical decision-making
papers.shortTitle: rCAST score in young children after arrest

papers.title: A Bayesian learning approach for drone coverage network: A case study on cardiac arrest in Scotland
papers.summary: Bayesian optimisation of a drone-assisted AED delivery network using geographically referenced Scottish cardiac arrest data — station placement driven by OHCA survival probability and existing EMS coverage, with cost-effectiveness analysis suggesting drone AED delivery is cost-effective and could meaningfully improve response coverage in rural areas with long ambulance response times.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Modelling study from Scotland — the rural-coverage logic translates to Australian contexts, but there's no local feasibility or trial data here.
papers.design: Bayesian optimisation modelling of drone-assisted AED network
papers.n: Geographically referenced Scottish cardiac arrest data (number not reported)
papers.finding: Optimised station placement based on OHCA survival probability suggests drone-assisted AED delivery is expected to be cost-effective on QALY grounds and could significantly improve response coverage in rural and urban areas with long ambulance response times
papers.caveat: Modelling study, not an implemented or evaluated service
papers.shortTitle: Drone AED network modelling for Scotland

papers.title: Barriers to dispatcher-assisted CPR are associated with delayed bystander CPR and worse outcomes in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a retrospective cohort study
papers.summary: Retrospective cohort of 3,263 transcribed Swedish 112 calls linked to the national cardiac arrest registry quantified barriers to dispatcher-assisted CPR after the dispatcher recognised arrest — 43.7% of calls hit at least one barrier (commonest: inability to move the patient), bystander CPR reached 85% in barrier-free calls but stayed below 50% with three or more, and any barrier was associated with lower ROSC (adjusted RR 0.89) and 30-day survival (adjusted RR 0.57).
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — no new drugs or skills, pure call-handling and bystander CPR quality improvement any Australian service, ACTAS included, can act on in dispatch protocols
papers.design: Retrospective cohort linking 112 call transcripts to national registry
papers.n: 3,263 adults with OHCA in Sweden
papers.finding: 43.7% of calls had ≥1 barrier to dispatcher-assisted CPR (commonest: inability to move the patient, 55.8% of barrier-present calls). Bystander CPR reached 85% in barrier-free calls vs <50% with ≥3 barriers. Any barrier was associated with lower ROSC (adjusted RR 0.89, 95% CrI 0.81–0.98) and 30-day survival (adjusted RR 0.57, 95% CrI 0.46–0.71).
papers.caveat: Retrospective single-country (Swedish) data; residual confounding likely as barriers reflect caller/patient factors
papers.shortTitle: Dispatcher CPR barriers delay bystander CPR, cut survival

papers.title: Nighttime human-supervised drone-delivered automated external defibrillators: a quasi-experimental mixed-methods feasibility study
papers.summary: Quasi-experimental mixed-methods study of 24 human-supervised drone flights delivering a 480 g CellAED over 877 m in a semi-urban area — all flights completed without safety incidents and night flight times matched day (mean ~140 s vs ~136 s, p=0.43), though pilots reported markedly higher cognitive workload and environmental complexity after dark.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — promising OHCA response tech but only proven under controlled early-night, open-area conditions; not an ACTAS capability, would be a system-level procurement and regulatory step
papers.design: Quasi-experimental mixed-methods feasibility study (24 controlled flights)
papers.n: 24 human-supervised drone flights (12 day, 12 night) by advanced-rated paramedic pilots
papers.finding: All flights completed without safety incidents; night flight times matched day (139.92 ± 14.16 s vs 136.00 ± 8.71 s; p=0.43), but pilots reported markedly higher cognitive workload and environmental complexity at night.
papers.caveat: Small number of flights in controlled, early-night, open-area conditions — not real OHCA response
papers.shortTitle: Night drone AED delivery feasible but workload high

papers.title: When ambulances are not enough: An interview-based needs assessment of governance and accountability gaps in prehospital emergency care in Hawassa, Ethiopia
papers.summary: Qualitative needs assessment using the WHO prehospital assessment tool across 15 interviews with EMS and health bureau leaders in Hawassa, Ethiopia identified six recurring barriers — infrastructure, medicines/equipment, communication, community perceptions, workforce and, cutting across all of them, unclear governance and accountability — leaving services functioning as interfacility transport rather than true prehospital care.
papers.relevance: 🔴 Low — valuable LMIC systems insight but nothing applicable to ACTAS operations or an established governance structure
papers.design: Qualitative interview-based needs assessment using WHO prehospital assessment tool
papers.n: 15 interviews with EMS leaders, administrators and health bureau coordinators in Hawassa, Ethiopia
papers.finding: Six recurring barriers identified: infrastructure, medicines/equipment shortages, communication gaps, community perceptions, workforce limitations and structural weaknesses, with unclear governance and accountability as a central cross-cutting barrier; services often function as interfacility transport rather than prehospital care.
papers.caveat: Small, single-city qualitative study in a low-income setting — limited generalisability to Australia
papers.shortTitle: Governance gaps cripple Ethiopian prehospital care

papers.title: Association Between Early Prehospital Administration Antibiotic and 28-Day Mortality in Sepsis
papers.summary: Thai observational cohort of 364 adults with suspected sepsis testing prehospital antibiotics — prehospital administration was associated with lower adjusted 28-day mortality (ARR 8.9%, 95% CI 0.8–17.1; aOR 0.51) and antibiotics ~125 minutes sooner, but scene times ran 8.5 minutes longer.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Single-centre Thai observational design with residual confounding likely; ACTAS CMG 38 (Sepsis) has no prehospital antibiotic step — ceftriaxone is scoped to suspected meningococcal disease (CMG 38A) only, so adoption would need a guideline change.
papers.design: Single-centre observational cohort
papers.n: 364 adults with suspected sepsis
papers.finding: Prehospital antibiotics (154/364) associated with lower 28-day mortality (25.9% vs 28.1%; adjusted ARR 8.9%, 95% CI 0.8–17.1; aOR 0.51) and antibiotics given ~125 minutes sooner, at the cost of ~8.5 minutes longer scene time
papers.caveat: Single-centre observational design; residual confounding likely despite adjustment
papers.shortTitle: Prehospital antibiotics earlier in sepsis

papers.title: Prehospital management and outcomes of traumatic cardiac arrest in older adults: a French nationwide registry study
papers.summary: French national registry study of 5,595 traumatic cardiac arrests comparing older (≥65) with younger adults — older patients achieved ROSC more often (22.5% vs 18.6%) but 30-day survival was lower (0.5% vs 1.2%), leading the authors to argue age alone shouldn't preclude resuscitation though a concurrent medical cause should be sought
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — haemorrhage control and chest-injury care are AP scope (CMG 17), but the interventions studied — prehospital fluid resuscitation and thoracostomy — sit beyond ACTAS practice; the age-based prognosis message transfers, the techniques don't
papers.design: Multicentre national registry cohort
papers.n: 5,595 adults with traumatic cardiac arrest (1,346 aged ≥65)
papers.finding: Older patients achieved ROSC more often (22.5% vs 18.6%; OR 1.22, 95% CI 1.03–1.45) but had lower 30-day survival (0.5% vs 1.2%; OR 0.34, 95% CI 0.15–0.81); fewer trauma-specific interventions, e.g. thoracostomy 15.2% vs 23.9%
papers.caveat: Registry data from the French system; residual confounding including unmeasured injury severity and medical causes of arrest
papers.shortTitle: Traumatic arrest in older adults

papers.title: Association of a smartphone-based CPR assistance system with prehospital outcomes in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a pre–post observational study in Bangkok
papers.summary: Before–after study of 615 OHCA patients after the MySOS smartphone bystander-CPR app launched in Bangkok — post-implementation ROSC probability rose ~6 percentage points, but 24-hour and discharge survival showed no significant improvement
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — app-based bystander alerting isn't part of ACTAS's extracted pathways — relevant to local OHCA system debates rather than on-road practice, and the authors themselves caution the association isn't causal
papers.design: Retrospective uncontrolled before–after observational study with IPTW
papers.n: 615 OHCA patients in Bangkok (340 pre-, 275 post-implementation)
papers.finding: Post-implementation ROSC probability higher (adjusted RD 6.28%, 95% CI 1.69–10.86; p=0.007), but RR not significant (1.21, 95% CI 0.78–1.89) and no significant improvement in 24-hour or discharge survival
papers.caveat: Uncontrolled before–after design without patient-level confirmation of actual app use; temporal confounding likely
papers.shortTitle: Smartphone CPR app: ROSC up, survival not

papers.title: Differences in the rates of bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest resulting in favourable neurological outcomes according to the regional deprivation index
papers.summary: Analysis of 184,727 Korean OHCA cases found bystander CPR rates were lowest in the most deprived regions, yet its association with good neurological outcome was strongest there (aOR 1.56 vs 1.31–1.34 in better-off regions)
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — pure epidemiology with no practice change for ACTAS, but a useful equity lens for Australian community CPR programs targeting disadvantaged suburbs
papers.design: National registry analysis with multivariable logistic regression
papers.n: 184,727 adults with presumed cardiac OHCA (61.0% received bystander CPR)
papers.finding: Bystander CPR rates were lowest in high-deprivation regions (57.9% vs 62.6% in low-deprivation), yet the association with favourable neurological outcome was strongest there (aOR 1.56, 95% CI 1.23–1.99 vs 1.31–1.34; significant interaction)
papers.caveat: Korean registry data; observational associations may not generalise to Australian systems
papers.shortTitle: Bystander CPR benefits greatest in deprived areas

papers.title: In-hospital cardiac arrest in a resource-limited emergency department in Somalia: Outcomes and priorities for resuscitation system development
papers.summary: Prospective study of 240 in-hospital arrests in a Mogadishu ED — ROSC 5.8%, survival past 24 hours 1.3%, with CPR initiation documented in only 15% of cases, underlining system gaps rather than treatment questions
papers.relevance: 🔴 Low transferability — resource-limited hospital setting with a trauma-dominated case mix — little transfers to a well-resourced two-tier ambulance service
papers.design: Prospective single-centre observational study
papers.n: 240 adult in-hospital cardiac arrests in a Mogadishu ED
papers.finding: ROSC achieved in 5.8% and survival beyond 24 hours in 1.3%; CPR initiation documented in only 14.6% and emergency response activation in 22.6%
papers.caveat: Single resource-limited in-hospital setting with incomplete documentation; not generalisable and not prehospital
papers.shortTitle: In-hospital arrests in resource-limited Somalia

papers.title: A Causal Model for Prehospital Blood Transfusion and Mortality in Traumatic Hemorrhagic Shock
papers.summary: Methodology paper building an expert-refined causal model for prehospital blood transfusion trials in traumatic haemorrhagic shock — maps confounders (system times, training, units available) and mediators so future studies can actually isolate a treatment effect against crystalloid
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — blood products aren't in the extracted ACTAS formulary — would need a guideline change to adopt; QAS, AV, SJWA and NSWA already run prehospital blood programs, so how this evidence matures matters interstate
papers.design: Expert-refined causal modelling methodology paper
papers.n: Not applicable (no patients; multidisciplinary expert stakeholder review)
papers.finding: Developed a causal model linking prehospital blood transfusion to mortality in traumatic haemorrhagic shock, mapping confounders (system times, clinician training, blood availability), mediators (physiologic and system) and colliders to guide future studies
papers.caveat: Methodological framework only; no patient data or treatment effect estimates
papers.shortTitle: Causal model for prehospital blood trials

papers.title: Prehospital Whole Blood Transfusion During Medically Directed Rescue of an Entrapped Trauma Patient: A Case Report
papers.summary: Case report of an entrapped trauma patient after a motor vehicle collision receiving advanced airway management, finger thoracostomies and multiple units of low-titre O-positive whole blood during a prolonged multi-agency extrication — the blood came via the regional prehospital program supporting a physician response team
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — whole blood isn't carried by ACTAS (it is by QAS, AV, SJWA and NSWA); the extended-extrication field-care picture is worth reading for major-incident planning
papers.design: Case report
papers.n: One entrapped trauma patient
papers.finding: Prolonged multi-agency rescue of an entrapped patient with advanced airway management, finger thoracostomies and multiple units of low-titre O-positive whole blood for haemorrhagic shock, using prehospital blood program stock redistributed to a physician response team
papers.caveat: Single case report; no outcome or comparative data
papers.shortTitle: Whole blood during prolonged entrapment rescue

papers.title: Practice Patterns and Performance of Pediatric Air Medical Tracheal Intubation: A National Multisite Cohort Study
papers.summary: US national cohort of 1,040 paediatric air medical intubations — 86.5% first-pass success overall but only 69.1% in infants under 1, with ketamine the commonest induction agent and substantial site-to-site variation
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — RSI is ICP-only at ACTAS and infants aren't intubated prehospital here; etomidate isn't carried and rocuronium isn't either, so the drug mix is overseas practice — but the infant first-pass numbers are a sharp caution for any advanced paediatric airway pathway
papers.design: Retrospective national multisite cohort
papers.n: 1,040 paediatric air medical intubations at 39 US sites
papers.finding: First-pass success 86.5% (898/1,038) and overall success 93.3%; only 69.1% first-pass success in infants <1 year vs 88.7% in adolescents, with less frequent post-intubation ETCO2 documentation; ketamine most common induction agent (43.5%); substantial site variation
papers.caveat: US air medical cohort with retrospective data and only 8.6% video laryngoscopy documentation; may not generalise to Australian systems
papers.shortTitle: Paediatric air medical intubation performance

papers.title: Efficacy and Safety of Ventilator Assisted Preoxygenation for Intubation in Two Australian Emergency Departments: A Retrospective Cohort Study
papers.summary: Australian retrospective cohort of 116 patients intubated with ventilator-assisted preoxygenation (VAPOX) in two EDs — 78% achieved first-pass success without hypoxaemia, but half had at least one complication and 36% became hypotensive after intubation
papers.relevance: 🟢 High transferability — Australian data directly relevant to preoxygenation before intubation (CMG 3B, ICP-only) — VAPOX is an ED ventilator setup, but the oxygenation physiology and complication profile inform how ICPs prep a physiologically difficult airway
papers.design: Retrospective cohort study in two Australian EDs
papers.n: 116 adults intubated with VAPOX
papers.finding: First-pass success without hypoxaemia in 78% (95% CI 69–84%); overall first-pass success 91%; hypoxaemia 17%; post-intubation hypotension 36%; no aspiration; respiratory failure reduced success (OR 0.14, 95% CI 0.04–0.52)
papers.caveat: Retrospective design with no comparator group
papers.shortTitle: VAPOX preoxygenation in ED intubation

papers.title: Quantification of blood-based neurovascular unit biomarkers: an analytical platform comparison study
papers.summary: Platform-comparison study of post-arrest HIBI biomarkers (GFAP, Nf-L, tau, UCH-L1) — lab-grade analyser results correlated highly with each other, but the point-of-care i-STAT agreed poorly, so prognostication thresholds can't be shared across devices
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — prognostication happens hospital-side after ACTAS transports ROSC patients (CMG 4A) — useful background on why biomarker numbers aren't portable, not road-practice changing
papers.design: Post hoc cross-platform analytical comparison within a prospective observational cohort
papers.n: 32 critically ill patients after withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy
papers.finding: GFAP, Nf-L, tau and UCH-L1 highly correlated between Simoa HD-X and ARGO HT (all r ≥ 0.97), but i-STAT Alinity agreement was poor-to-moderate for GFAP (ICC 0.25) and poor-to-good for UCH-L1 (ICC 0.60)
papers.caveat: Small sample and post hoc design; not a clinical outcome study
papers.shortTitle: Post-arrest biomarker platforms don't agree

papers.title: SGLT-2 Use and Hypoglycemic Ketoacidosis
papers.summary: Case report of severe hypoglycaemic ketoacidosis in an SGLT2 inhibitor user requiring insulin — a reminder these agents can produce ketosis with atypical glucose readings that muddle the diabetic-emergencies picture
papers.relevance: 🟢 High transferability — no new drug or skill needed — pure recognition: a growing number of patients are on SGLT2 inhibitors, and a BGL that doesn't fit the picture (CMG 10) deserves a second look
papers.design: Case report
papers.n: 1 patient
papers.finding: Severe hypoglycaemic, nondiabetic ketoacidosis in an SGLT-2 inhibitor user requiring insulin treatment
papers.caveat: Single case, cannot establish frequency or causality
papers.shortTitle: SGLT-2 inhibitor hypoglycaemic ketoacidosis

papers.title: Medical Management of Aortic Emergencies in Critical Care Transport
papers.summary: Cohort of 1,530 aortic emergencies in US critical care transport — esmolol, labetalol and nicardipine strategies hit HR/BP targets at similar rates, with esmolol alone showing the highest hypotension incidence (9.3%) and labetalol alone the lowest (2.1%)
papers.relevance: 🔴 Low transferability — critical-care transport scope built on infusions; beta-blockers aren't in the extracted ACTAS formulary (only QAS carries them interstate) — background awareness only
papers.design: Retrospective cohort of US critical care transport encounters
papers.n: 1,530 adults with aortic emergencies
papers.finding: All drug strategies achieved target HR/SBP similarly; hypotension lowest with labetalol alone (2.1%) and highest with esmolol (9.3%); esmolol/nicardipine combination had lowest tachycardia (11.0%)
papers.caveat: Retrospective design; US critical care transport setting not directly applicable to Australian paramedic practice
papers.shortTitle: Aortic emergencies: HR/BP drugs in transport

papers.title: Management of Patients with Medetomidine Withdrawal During Interfacility Transfer
papers.summary: Cohort of 100 interfacility transfers on dexmedetomidine infusions for medetomidine withdrawal — transports were largely uncomplicated but profound hypertension was common (39%), reflecting the growing US opioid-supply adulterant problem
papers.relevance: 🔴 Low transferability — dexmedetomidine isn't carried by ACTAS and medetomidine adulteration is a US drug-supply phenomenon — relevant only if such an infused patient ever moves through ACT interfacility transfer
papers.design: Retrospective observational cohort of interfacility critical care transfers
papers.n: 100 non-intubated adults receiving dexmedetomidine infusion for suspected medetomidine withdrawal
papers.finding: 78% hypertensive (SBP >140) and 39% profoundly hypertensive during transfer; 10% needed dexmedetomidine titration, 12% antiemetics, 9% sedatives; no alternate sedative infusions required
papers.caveat: Retrospective single-agency US cohort; medetomidine adulteration not established in Australia
papers.shortTitle: Medetomidine withdrawal transfers on dexmedetomidine

papers.title: Intranasal Dexmedetomidine for Paediatric Procedural Sedation in the Emergency Department: A Single‐Centre Retrospective Observational Cohort Study
papers.summary: Townsville cohort of 114 children given intranasal dexmedetomidine for ED procedural sedation — effective as a sole agent in 78%, adverse events in 13% (mostly mild bradycardia), but ED stays ran long at a median 395 minutes
papers.relevance: 🔴 Low transferability — intranasal dexmedetomidine isn't in the ACTAS formulary and procedural sedation stays in ED hands — interesting Australian evidence should a scope debate ever arrive
papers.design: Single-centre retrospective observational cohort after guideline implementation
papers.n: 114 children aged 1–16 years in Townsville ED
papers.finding: IN dexmedetomidine successful as sole agent in 78.1% (95% CI 69.6–84.7%); adverse events 13.2%, mostly mild bradycardia; median ED length of stay 395 min; younger age associated with higher success (aOR 0.86 per year)
papers.caveat: Single-centre retrospective design with incomplete documentation of sedation depth and satisfaction
papers.shortTitle: Intranasal dexmedetomidine paediatric sedation

papers.title: Redesigning 9-1-1 Paramedic Pathways: Evaluation of the IMPACC Model of Care
papers.summary: Evaluation of 7,382 encounters under Toronto's IMPACC model, which lets specially trained paramedics redirect lower-acuity 911 callers — activated encounters had transport rates of 36% vs 82% for others (still 43% vs 79% after matching) but added roughly 24 minutes on scene, with 4% re-contact at 72 hours
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — treat-and-refer isn't in ACTAS's extracted model — but if the ACT ever debates widening paramedic-led pathways for low-acuity triple-zero callers, this is the strongest implementation evidence yet, warts and all
papers.design: Retrospective observational cohort implementation evaluation with exact-matched comparison
papers.n: 7,382 9-1-1 encounters attended by IMPACC-trained paramedics
papers.finding: IMPACC activated in 9.9% of encounters; activated encounters had lower transport rates than non-activated (36.4% vs 81.7%) and than matched controls (42.9% vs 79.2%); time on task longer (90.0 vs 66.5 min); 72-hour repeat contact 4.0%
papers.caveat: Observational Canadian 9-1-1 system; marked paramedic-level heterogeneity (ICC 0.33) and declining activation over time
papers.shortTitle: IMPACC paramedic model cuts ED transport

papers.title: Differences in EMS Calls, Delays, and Payer Types in U.S. Southern Border Counties and Non-Border Counties
papers.summary: Comparison of 421,877 EMS encounters in US border versus matched non-border counties — border areas carried more severe trauma and environmental exposures (25.5% vs 8.2%) alongside larger response and scene delays
papers.relevance: 🔴 Low transferability — US border-specific system pressures with no Australian analogue — descriptive interest only
papers.design: Retrospective analysis of national EMS registry data with matched county comparison
papers.n: 421,877 EMS encounters across eight rural US counties (242,029 border; 179,848 comparison)
papers.finding: Border counties had more severe trauma or environmental exposure cases (25.5% vs 8.2%), more falls from ≥20 feet, and moderate-to-large differences in payer type, response and scene delays
papers.caveat: US-specific border setting; secondary data analysis with unadjusted comparisons
papers.shortTitle: US border counties: more trauma, more delays

papers.title: Medicolegal Statements by Emergency Clinicians: ‘A How’ to Guide
papers.summary: Practical guide on the statement types Australian emergency clinicians may be asked to provide for police, coroners and criminal proceedings — they're statements of fact rather than opinion, and structure and clarity matter
papers.relevance: 🟢 High transferability — directly useful for Australian paramedics — medicolegal statements are a real part of the job, and Michael Eburn writes from deep ambulance-law knowledge
papers.design: Practical guidance article
papers.n: Not reported
papers.shortTitle: How to write medicolegal statements

papers.title: The Once‐Conventional 48‐h Elective Cardioversion Threshold for “Recent‐Onset” Atrial Fibrillation Is No Longer Recommended
papers.summary: EMA commentary arguing the once-conventional 48-hour elective cardioversion threshold for recent-onset atrial fibrillation is no longer supported
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — cardioversion is AP scope, but this is an ED-practice argument rather than a prehospital study — worth tracking where Australian EDs land before any guideline ripple reaches ambulance CMGs
papers.design: Journal commentary
papers.shortTitle: 48-hour AF cardioversion threshold abandoned

papers.title: Feasibility of multi-domain data acquisition in patients at risk for hypoxic-ischemic brain injury following cardiac arrest: a prospective cohort study
papers.summary: Canadian prospective feasibility study testing whether multi-domain prognostication data (biomarkers, transcranial Doppler, EEG, neuroimaging, six-month outcomes) can be collected in 30 adults after cardiac arrest — day-1 biomarkers (97%) and CT/MRI were feasible, but serial transcranial Doppler (77%), day-7 biomarker sampling (71%) and the complete six-month multidomain battery (33%) fell short, with remote or proxy-assisted follow-up improving outcome ascertainment.
papers.relevance: 🔴 Low — ICU-phase prognostication research methods, nothing actionable prehospital
papers.design: Prospective feasibility cohort study
papers.n: 30 adults admitted to critical care after cardiac arrest
papers.finding: Day-1 biomarkers obtained in 97%, CT/MRI in 100%; but transcranial Doppler in 77%, day-7 biomarkers in 71%, and complete six-month in-person multidomain battery in 4/12 (33%) hospital survivors; remote or proxy-assisted follow-up improved outcome ascertainment.
papers.caveat: Small single-centre feasibility sample; no outcome conclusions.
papers.shortTitle: Multi-domain post-arrest prognostication data feasibility

papers.title: Adaptation of the CONOCES-BLS scale to citizens: evidence of content validity and preliminary psychometric evaluation
papers.summary: Spanish methodological study adapting the CONOCES-BLS knowledge scale for adult laypersons via Delphi expert consensus and pilot testing — content validity was strong (expert agreement above 0.90 on every item, Krippendorff coefficients 0.91–1.0) and internal consistency adequate (Cronbach's alpha 0.82), supporting its use for assessing community BLS knowledge pending further psychometric work.
papers.relevance: 🔴 Low — citizen-BLS education instrument, community training relevance only
papers.design: Methodological scale-adaptation study with Delphi panel and pilot testing
papers.n: Not reported
papers.finding: Content validity agreement >0.90 on every item (Krippendorff K* 0.91–1.0); pilot internal consistency Cronbach's alpha 0.82.
papers.caveat: Only preliminary psychometric evaluation; further validation needed.
papers.shortTitle: CONOCES-BLS scale adapted for citizens

papers.title: Emergency response with lights and sirens to patients with a suspected out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and a do-not-attempt-resuscitation order in the hospital record: a one-year observational study
papers.summary: One-year regional study of 1,695 lights-and-sirens dispatches for suspected OHCA in Southern Denmark — 15.7% involved a patient with a physician-issued hospital DNAR order that dispatchers and crews couldn't access, one-day mortality was 90.6% in that group, and the authors call for DNAR orders to be visible to emergency dispatch and prehospital providers.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Danish register and dispatch infrastructure differs, but the ethics and resource cost of resuscitating patients with documented DNAR orders is a system gap crews here will recognise
papers.design: Retrospective regional observational study
papers.n: 1,695 lights-and-sirens dispatches for suspected OHCA
papers.finding: 15.7% had a physician-issued hospital DNAR order; 47.4% of these recorded it as patient-requested; one-day mortality was 90.6% with DNAR versus 69.5% without (p<0.05).
papers.caveat: Single Danish region; DNAR orders only identifiable if documented in accessible records.
papers.shortTitle: DNAR orders missed in OHCA dispatches

papers.title: Implementation gap in prehospital termination-of-resuscitation policies for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with do-not-attempt-cardiopulmonary-resuscitation wishes in Japan: a nationwide survey
papers.summary: Nationwide Japanese survey of 561 fire departments — 47% had a prehospital termination-of-resuscitation policy for OHCA with DNACPR wishes, yet 52% of departments with evaluable data applied it to zero cases during 2024 despite encountering eligible patients, and departments with a policy transported far fewer arrests with ongoing CPR (46% vs 82%).
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Japanese DNACPR legislation limits direct transfer, but the policy-versus-practice implementation gap applies to any TOR guideline including ours under CMG 4
papers.design: Nationwide cross-sectional survey of fire departments and medical control councils
papers.n: 561 of 791 fire departments (71%)
papers.finding: 47% had a TOR policy for OHCA with DNACPR wishes; among 151 departments with evaluable data, 52% applied the policy to zero cases in 2024; departments with a policy transported fewer arrests with ongoing CPR (46% vs 82%; adjusted OR 0.17, 95% CI 0.09–0.30).
papers.caveat: Japanese system; survey-based self-reported data and low response from some council levels.
papers.shortTitle: DNACPR termination policies poorly applied in Japan

papers.title: Association between destination hospital level and outcomes in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest patients under a dispatch-guided transport system: a population-based study in Nagoya, Japan
papers.summary: Population-based cohort of 12,663 OHCA transports in Nagoya under a dispatch-guided destination system — transport to critical care medical centres showed no association with favourable one-month neurological outcomes overall, was linked to lower one-month survival in non-shockable rhythms (OR 0.66), and only refractory shockable rhythms showed a possible survival edge (19.7% vs 3.3%, imprecise estimate).
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Japanese dispatch-guided destination system differs from ACT transport pathways; findings are largely null and the refractory VF signal is hypothesis-generating only
papers.design: Retrospective population-based cohort with IPTW analysis
papers.n: 12,663 OHCA transports in Nagoya City
papers.finding: No association between transport to critical care medical centres and favourable one-month neurological outcome overall; lower one-month survival with non-shockable rhythm (OR 0.66, 95% CI 0.46–0.95); exploratory higher survival in refractory shockable rhythm (19.7% vs 3.3%), imprecise estimate.
papers.caveat: Retrospective, residual confounding despite IPTW; exploratory subgroup estimates imprecise.
papers.shortTitle: Transport destination not linked to OHCA outcomes

papers.title: Systematic Review of Pediatric Ketamine in Emergency Department Procedural Sedation: Frequency and Predictors of Adverse Events
papers.summary: Systematic review of 20 studies covering 67,871 children having IV ketamine procedural sedation in EDs — no deaths or permanent adverse outcomes, sentinel events pooled at about 1 in 11,558 sedations, serious adverse events 0.34%, with age ≥10, upper respiratory infection and opioid co-administration modest predictors while ASA status and benzodiazepine co-administration were not.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — ED-based procedural sedation rather than prehospital practice, but reassuring safety data for a heavily used AP formulary drug
papers.design: Systematic review of studies with ≥250 children
papers.n: 58,752 children receiving IV ketamine in EDs across 20 studies
papers.finding: No deaths or permanent adverse outcomes; pooled sentinel events 0.0041% (~1 in 24,390 sedations); serious adverse events 0.33%; predictors of serious events were age ≥10 years, upper respiratory infection and co-administered opioids.
papers.caveat: Heterogeneity across studies; ED (not prehospital) setting; rare-event estimates imprecise.
papers.shortTitle: Paediatric IV ketamine sedation very safe

papers.title: Emergency Department Boarding for Older Adults: The Impact of Geography, Temporal Trends, and Dementia Status
papers.summary: US national survey analysis of 4.45 million admissions of adults aged ≥65 (2015–2022) — 85% boarded ≥2 hours in the ED, mean boarding time rose from 138 minutes in 2018 to 343 minutes in 2022 and roughly 501 minutes for patients with Alzheimer's-related dementia, with the worst growth in metropolitan areas and among those ≥75.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — US access-block data we can't act on directly, but the off-stretcher delays it describes are familiar at Canberra Hospital
papers.design: Cross-sectional analysis of national survey data (NHAMCS 2015–2022)
papers.n: 4.45 million weighted hospital admissions of adults aged ≥65 with complete data
papers.finding: 85.2% boarded ≥2 hours; mean boarding time rose from 138 minutes in 2018 to 343 minutes in 2022, reaching 501 minutes (95% CI -20 to 1,022) with Alzheimer's disease-related dementia; each calendar year associated with 3.2% increase in 4-hour boarding and 15.3 extra minutes.
papers.caveat: US survey data with wide confidence intervals, especially the dementia subgroup estimate; in-hospital system issue.
papers.shortTitle: Rising ED boarding for older adults

papers.title: Trends in the incidence and outcomes of cardiopulmonary resuscitation-induced consciousness in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a retrospective study
papers.summary: Ambulance Victoria registry study of 43,402 adult OHCA cases (2008–2024) identifying CPR-induced consciousness — 1,438 patients (3.3%), with annual incidence rising (IRR 1.083, 95% CI 1.07–1.10) across all arrest rhythms, and CPRIC associated with improved survival to hospital discharge.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Australian (VACAR) prehospital cardiac arrest data within AP scope (CMG 4); directly relevant to crews running arrests.
papers.design: Retrospective registry cohort study (Victorian Ambulance Cardiac Arrest Registry)
papers.n: 43,402 adults with OHCA (2008–2024); 1,438 with CPRIC
papers.finding: CPRIC occurred in 3.3% of OHCA; annual incidence increased over time (IRR 1.083, 95% CI 1.07–1.10) across all rhythms; CPRIC associated with improved survival to hospital discharge.
papers.caveat: Retrospective registry data; association between CPRIC and survival may reflect favourable patient physiology rather than causation.
papers.shortTitle: CPR-induced consciousness rising in OHCA

papers.title: Selection bias introduced in a randomized clinical trial due to employee instigated deletion of newborn resuscitation videos
papers.summary: Norwegian analysis of the NeoBeat RCT testing whether anonymous staff deletion of resuscitation videos introduced selection bias — after the anonymous opt-out, enrolled newborns had significantly higher Apgar scores, shorter ventilation and fewer admissions, and the trial was terminated halfway without power to conclude on its outcomes.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — methodological finding on a neonatal resuscitation RCT rather than a practice change; useful caution for interpreting newborn resus evidence (CMG 5B context).
papers.design: Analysis of selection bias within a randomised clinical trial (NeoBeat, Norway)
papers.n: 9,909 newborns ≥34 weeks gestation (7,343 before, 2,566 after anonymous opt-out); 237 with video data
papers.finding: After anonymous video deletion was introduced, enrolled newborns had significantly higher Apgar scores, shorter ventilation duration and fewer admissions; the trial was terminated halfway without power to conclude on its outcomes.
papers.caveat: Hospital-based newborn resuscitation trial; analysis limited by only 171 vs 66 video cases available.
papers.shortTitle: Anonymous video deletion biased newborn RCT

papers.title: Prehospital management of pain associated with acute complications of Sickle Cell Disease: a preliminary nationwide cross-sectional study
papers.journal: The American Journal of Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: US nationwide cross-section of 10,023 9-1-1 ALS encounters for sickle cell disease complications in 2023 — pain scores documented in 73% but only 13.5% received any analgesia (11.7% opioids), and among patients scoring ≥7/10, contact times ≥20 min were associated with roughly five-fold more IV access and ten-fold more analgesia/opioid administration.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — US administrative data and associations, not causation, but vaso-occlusive pain undertreatment maps onto ACTAS pain management (CMG 2) where fentanyl IN and methoxyflurane are in scope.
papers.design: Nationwide cross-sectional study of ALS encounters
papers.n: 10,023 EMS encounters for sickle cell disease complications (5.2% paediatric)
papers.finding: Pain scores documented in 73.0%; analgesia given in 13.5% (11.7% opioids); among patients scoring ≥7/10, contact times ≥20 min were associated with roughly five-fold more IV access and ten-fold more analgesia/opioid administration.
papers.caveat: US dataset; cross-sectional design cannot establish causation and documentation bias likely.
papers.shortTitle: Low analgesia rates in sickle cell EMS pain

papers.title: Comparative efficacy of fluid resuscitation strategies in a rat model of traumatic cardiac arrest
papers.summary: Rat model of traumatic cardiac arrest (30% haemorrhage plus asphyxia) comparing four fluids after ROSC found 96-hour survival of 90% with whole blood, 80% with HES, 60% with lactated Ringer's and just 30% with normal saline — crystalloids prolonged survival without improving haemodynamics.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — preclinical rat data only, and whole blood isn't carried by ACTAS (QAS, AV, SJWA and NSWA all carry it), but the anti-crystalloid signal lines up with clinical TCA practice.
papers.design: Randomised animal experimental study (rat haemorrhage + asphyxia TCA model)
papers.n: Rats randomised to normal saline, lactated Ringer's, HES or whole blood after ROSC
papers.finding: 96-hour survival: whole blood 90%, HES 80%, lactated Ringer's 60%, normal saline 30%; whole blood and HES improved haemodynamics and reduced tissue injury versus saline.
papers.caveat: Small animal model of haemorrhage plus asphyxia; translation to human prehospital TCA uncertain.
papers.shortTitle: Fluids in traumatic cardiac arrest: rat model

papers.title: Large language models fail to reliably predict emergent catheterization laboratory activation from prehospital electrocardiograms
papers.summary: Retrospective test of three multimodal LLMs against real cardiology cath-lab activation decisions on 615 prehospital ECGs found the best (Gemini, 95.3% sensitivity) had 9.4% specificity, and the standard ECG machine algorithm beat all three LLMs overall — general-purpose LLMs aren't reliable for STEMI pathway activation.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — prehospital 12-lead interpretation is core AP scope; a solid caution against using an LLM chatbot as an ECG second opinion.
papers.design: Retrospective diagnostic accuracy study comparing three multimodal LLMs and ECG machine algorithm against cardiology decisions
papers.n: 615 prehospital ECGs from 270 EMS encounters
papers.finding: Gemini: sensitivity 95.3% but specificity 9.4%; ChatGPT and Claude sensitivity 68.1% and 67.2% with specificity 42.3% and 46.5%; ECG machine algorithm sensitivity 67.7%, specificity 64.2% — outperforming all LLMs overall.
papers.caveat: Retrospective single reference standard (cardiology activation) and no Australian validation; LLM performance may change with newer models.
papers.shortTitle: LLMs unreliable for cath-lab activation ECGs

papers.title: Standing chest compressions: simulation-based development and evaluation of a clinically applicable height adjustment approach
papers.summary: Simulation study with 30 participants compressing at seven working heights found knee-height bed or stretcher position gave the best compressions (52.7 mm mean depth, 80.6% correct depth), with positions 15–20 cm above knee height significantly worse.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — zero-cost CPR quality tweak applicable to any stretcher job, though manikin data with a small sample.
papers.design: Prospective simulation study of chest compression quality at seven working heights
papers.n: 30 participants (10 healthcare professionals, 20 medical students)
papers.finding: Knee-height bed/stretcher gave best compressions (mean depth 52.7 mm, 80.6% correct depth); heights 15–20 cm above knee height gave significantly lower compression depth; no difference between knee height, kneeling and lowest stretcher height.
papers.caveat: Simulation with manikins and no experienced-only paramedic cohort; compression quality may not translate to real resuscitations.
papers.shortTitle: Best height for standing compressions

papers.title: Implementation of a Structured Hot Debrief Tool in a Metropolitan ED: A Quality Improvement Study
papers.summary: Multi-site Australian quality improvement study of a structured hot debrief tool after critical events (46 debriefs across two metropolitan EDs) found 98% of attendees rated it psychologically safe and 59 of 60 found it useful, with themes surfacing system issues like medication dosing in rare events and staff safety during behavioural emergencies.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Australian setting and the model transfers directly to post-incident hot debriefs in ambulance crews.
papers.design: Multi-site quality improvement study with surveys and thematic analysis
papers.n: 46 hot debriefs across two metropolitan Australian EDs; 121 survey respondents
papers.finding: 98% of attendees reported debriefs were psychologically safe and 59 of 60 found them useful; themes identified included interdepartmental communication, medication dosing in rare events, staffing pressures and staff safety during behavioural emergencies.
papers.caveat: Quality improvement design without control group; ED setting, not prehospital; no data on downstream patient or staff outcomes.
papers.shortTitle: Hot debrief tool in metropolitan EDs

papers.title: A multinational cross-sectional survey on the use of AI-based voice assistance systems in emergency medical services
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: Multinational survey of 401 EMS clinicians in Germany, Norway and Switzerland exploring how AI-based voice assistance systems could be designed for prehospital care — respondents were technically proficient and already using digital tools mainly for documentation, knowledge access, hospital pre-notification and occupancy checks, with the study mapping requirements, expectations and implementation obstacles rather than testing clinical outcomes.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Acceptance/requirements survey only; no outcome data and no such system deployed in ACTAS, but it speaks directly to documentation and clinical-support workflows ACTAS shares.
papers.design: Multinational cross-sectional online survey (Germany, Norway, Switzerland)
papers.n: 401 EMS clinicians (587 responses, 186 excluded)
papers.finding: Digital tools used mainly for documentation, knowledge access, hospital pre-notification and occupancy checks; positive attitude towards voice assistants in missions; desired features include translation, patient history summarisation and documentation; key barriers are staff acceptance, funding and data protection.
papers.caveat: Survey of attitudes and requirements only — no clinical outcomes tested; European respondents may not generalise to Australian EMS.
papers.shortTitle: AI voice assistants in EMS: survey

papers.title: Effects of systemic mild hypercapnia on brain function in a refractory cardiac arrest model treated with extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation
papers.summary: Porcine refractory-VF arrest model (n=12) testing mild hypercapnia (PaCO2 50-55 mmHg) during ECPR — the hypercapnia group showed higher cerebral glucose (p=0.01) and lower caspase-8 expression, but no significant difference in brain tissue oxygen tension (49.9 vs 36.4 mmHg, p=0.13), intracranial pressure, EEG activity or serum brain-injury biomarkers.
papers.relevance: 🔴 Low — Animal lab model with molecular surrogate endpoints; ECPR is an ECMO-centre therapy well outside ACTAS prehospital scope.
papers.design: Randomised animal experimental study (porcine refractory VF arrest with ECPR)
papers.n: 12 pigs (6 normocapnia, 6 hypercapnia)
papers.finding: Hypercapnia group had higher cerebral glucose (p=0.01) and lower caspase-8 expression, but no significant difference in brain tissue oxygen tension (49.9 vs 36.4 mmHg, p=0.13), intracranial pressure, EEG activity or serum brain-injury biomarkers.
papers.caveat: Small animal model with only 6 animals per group; limited generalisability to human OHCA.
papers.shortTitle: Mild hypercapnia during ECPR in pigs

papers.title: Gelatin 4% and hydroxyethyl starch (130/0.42) impair clot formation in a human ex vivo whole-blood resuscitation model
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: Ex vivo human whole-blood model testing graded dilution with gelatin 4%, HES 130/0.42 and a balanced crystalloid — both colloids produced a clearly hypocoagulable ROTEM profile (prolonged clotting and clot formation times, reduced alpha-angle and maximum clot firmness, worst with HES) while the crystalloid alone stayed haemostatically neutral, and combining crystalloid with colloid dilution worsened the coagulopathy further.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — ex vivo lab findings, not clinical outcome data; ACTAS carries no colloids anyway, so it confirms current crystalloid-first fluid practice (CMG 14/39) rather than changing it.
papers.design: Ex vivo human whole-blood haemodilution model
papers.n: Human whole-blood samples diluted with gelatin 4%, HES 130/0.42 and balanced crystalloid (number of donors not reported)
papers.finding: Gelatin and HES produced a hypocoagulable ROTEM profile (prolonged clotting and clot formation times, reduced alpha-angle and MCF), worst with HES; balanced crystalloid alone remained haemostatically neutral, and crystalloid–colloid combinations showed non-linear, ratio-dependent coagulopathy.
papers.caveat: Ex vivo model without transfusion or clinical outcomes; donor sample size not reported.
papers.shortTitle: Gelatin and HES impair clot formation ex vivo

papers.title: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation quality during the transition in care from paramedic services to emergency department teams
papers.summary: Observational study of 35 OHCA transfers tracking CPR quality across the paramedic-to-ED handover — chest compression fraction (89–92%) and rate stayed guideline-compliant in every interval with no deterioration at transition, though compression depth was significantly deeper during paramedic intervals.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High transferability — direct evidence on paramedic-delivered CPR at handover, mapping to CMG 4 and everyday AP practice
papers.design: Retrospective observational study of defibrillator CPR metrics
papers.n: 35 adults with non-traumatic OHCA transported to a tertiary academic ED
papers.finding: Chest compression fraction (89–92%) and rate (109.9–117.5/min) were guideline compliant in all four intervals with no significant differences; compression depth was deeper in ED intervals (significantly higher than paramedic 5.8–5.9 cm).
papers.caveat: Small sample from a single tertiary ED; retrospective design.
papers.shortTitle: CPR quality maintained across paramedic-to-ED handover

papers.title: High‐Flow Nasal Oxygen Versus Conventional Oxygen Therapy and Non‐Invasive Ventilation for Acute Respiratory Failure in the Emergency Department: A Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis
papers.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 RCTs (1,955 patients) comparing high-flow nasal oxygen with conventional oxygen and NIV for acute respiratory failure in the ED — HFNO reduced intubation versus conventional oxygen (RR 0.61) but not versus NIV, with no clear benefit over either in COPD or acute heart failure.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — ED-based and HFNO isn't carried prehospital, but it shapes expectations for the respiratory distress patients we hand over on CPAP
papers.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of ED RCTs
papers.n: 17 RCTs, 1,955 adults with acute respiratory failure in the ED
papers.finding: HFNO reduced intubation and mechanical ventilation versus COT and NIV overall (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.47–0.88); versus COT alone RR 0.61 (0.41–0.91), but not versus NIV (RR 0.69, 0.42–1.14); benefit in undifferentiated ARF (RR 0.61, 0.41–0.93) but not COPD or acute heart failure.
papers.caveat: 10 of 17 studies had some risk-of-bias concerns and several analyses had notable heterogeneity.
papers.shortTitle: HFNO reduces intubation vs conventional oxygen

papers.title: Local Anaesthetic Dosing and Toxicity Knowledge in Australian Emergency Departments: A Multicentre Cross‐Sectional Survey
papers.summary: Multicentre survey of 114 emergency clinicians across three Queensland EDs — fewer than half correctly identified the recommended maximum dose for any of four local anaesthetics, 21.9% couldn't recall any features of LAST, and only 10.5% could state the lipid emulsion dosing regimen.
