papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — awareness-level for paramedics: lignocaine is ICP-only in ACTAS and lipid emulsion isn't carried, so management stays hospital-side
papers.design: Multicentre cross-sectional survey
papers.n: 114 emergency clinicians at three Queensland EDs
papers.finding: Fewer than half correctly identified the recommended maximum dose for any of four local anaesthetics (18.4% for bupivacaine to 48.2% for lidocaine); 21.9% could not recall any features of LAST; 57.9% identified lipid emulsion therapy but only 10.5% stated a dosing regimen.
papers.caveat: ED clinician survey only (not paramedics), self-reported recall, three Queensland sites.
papers.shortTitle: Knowledge gaps in local anaesthetic dosing and LAST

papers.title: Toxicological and Clinical Characteristics of Fatal Cases in the Emerging Drugs Network of Australia—Victoria (EDNAV) Clinical Registry 2020–2025
papers.summary: Case series of 46 deaths in Victoria's EDNAV toxicosurveillance registry (2020–2025) — 67% had out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, 91% were polysubstance with mixed stimulant–sedative patterns most common (methamphetamine 54%, heroin 52%), and hypoxic brain injury was the most frequent terminal complication.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High transferability — Australian data on arrests paramedics actually attend; reinforces that naloxone alone won't reverse mixed overdoses
papers.design: Retrospective observational case series from a state-wide toxicosurveillance registry
papers.n: 46 fatal cases (0.9% of 5,026 EDNAV presentations), Victoria 2020–2025
papers.finding: 89% male, median age 33 years; 67% had out-of-hospital cardiac arrest; 91% polysubstance (median 3 substances); methamphetamine (54%) and heroin (52%) most frequent detections; novel psychoactive substances 7.8% of detections; hypoxic brain injury the most common terminal complication (72%).
papers.caveat: Small case series limited to ED-presenting cases in one Australian state; survivor cases not analysed.
papers.shortTitle: Fatal illicit drug toxicity: mostly polysubstance OHCA

papers.title: Embedded Low‐Acuity Pathway in the Emergency Department: An Alternative to Stand‐Alone Urgent Care Services
papers.summary: Quasi-experimental study of an embedded ultra-low acuity pathway at Dubbo Base Hospital (n=4,798) — pathway availability halved did-not-wait rates (14.2%→6.9%), lifted seen-on-time and treatment performance, and cut mean ED length of stay by 51.7 minutes.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — system redesign rather than clinical care, but directly relevant to where low-acuity patients could be directed instead of transported
papers.design: Single-centre pragmatic quasi-experimental study
papers.n: 4,798 ATS Category 4–5 presentations at Dubbo Base Hospital (ULAP 2,178 vs standard care 2,620)
papers.finding: ULAP was associated with DNW falling from 14.2% to 6.9% (adjusted OR 0.43, 95% CI 0.35–0.53), seen-within-benchmark rising to 82.0% (OR 1.90, 1.64–2.20), ETP rising to 83.3% (OR 1.96, 1.69–2.28), and mean LOS 51.7 minutes shorter (95% CI −65.1 to −38.4).
papers.caveat: Single rural centre, quasi-experimental design with workforce-dependent exposure (risk of confounding).
papers.shortTitle: Embedded low-acuity pathway improves rural ED performance

papers.title: Early clinical predictors of amputation in frostbite: injury depth and extent for admission risk stratification
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: Retrospective cohort of 128 frostbite admissions in eastern Turkey — injury depth drove amputation risk (81.5% of third-degree injuries required amputation vs 1.6% of first/second-degree), and combining degree with %TBSA predicted amputation at admission (AUC 0.948), while inflammatory markers added nothing after adjustment.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — field-usable depth-and-extent assessment for exposure incidents, though genuine frostbite is rare around the ACT
papers.design: Retrospective single-centre cohort
papers.n: 128 patients admitted with frostbite to a tertiary hospital in eastern Turkey (98.4% foreign nationals)
papers.finding: Amputation in 42.2%; 81.5% of third-degree injuries required amputation versus 1.6% of first/second-degree (AUC 0.910); %TBSA independently associated with amputation (adjusted OR 2.23, 95% CI 1.59–3.32); combined degree and %TBSA predicted amputation at admission (AUC 0.948); PNI and NLR added no prognostic value.
papers.caveat: Retrospective single-centre cohort with a highly selected, predominantly migrant population; not prehospital or Australian.
papers.shortTitle: Frostbite depth and extent predict amputation

papers.title: Paediatric Procedural Sedation and Analgesia in Emergency Departments: A Delphi Consensus Study
papers.summary: Two-round Delphi consensus of 28 paediatric emergency clinicians from 23 Spanish centres — strong agreement on monitoring standards, staffing and safety requirements for paediatric procedural sedation, with ketamine the preferred agent for painful procedures.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — ketamine is in the ACTAS formulary and the safety principles carry over, but this is ED procedural sedation, not prehospital protocol
papers.design: Modified two-round Delphi consensus study
papers.n: 28 paediatric emergency clinicians from 23 Spanish centres
papers.finding: Strong consensus (≥70% agreement) on minimum safety requirements, monitoring standards, staffing competencies and organisational priorities; ketamine preferred for painful procedures, with variation in drug choice for less invasive or imaging procedures.
papers.caveat: Spanish expert panel only; consensus reflects opinion, not outcome evidence.
papers.shortTitle: Delphi consensus on paediatric procedural sedation

papers.title: Prehospital transfusion requirements in severe trauma: A multicenter, retrospective estimate of requirements
papers.summary: Multicentre French retrospective study applying the ABC score across four Paris-region prehospital services to estimate demand for prehospital blood — 27 of 139 severe trauma patients (19.7%) met ABC ≥2 with prehospital intervention time >20 min and median total prehospital time of 79 min, only 67% of those eligible received TXA, and 5 arrested prehospital, leading the authors to argue prehospital transfusion should not remain a rarity.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Blood products and TXA are not in the extracted ACTAS formulary — adoption would need a guideline change — though QAS, AV, SJWA and NSWA already carry blood products.
papers.design: Multicentre retrospective observational cohort
papers.n: 139 severe trauma patients from 5,921 missions across four Paris-region prehospital services
papers.finding: 27 (19.7%, 95% CI 13.7-26.8%) met ABC ≥2 with prehospital intervention time >20 min; median total intervention time 79 min; 67% of eligible received TXA; five had prehospital cardiac arrest
papers.caveat: Retrospective with assumed eligibility criteria; French physician-staffed system limits generalisability
papers.shortTitle: One in five severe trauma cases may need prehospital blood

papers.title: 2026 Systematic Review of Evidence-Based Guidelines for Prehospital Care
papers.summary: The 2026 update of the systematic review appraising evidence-based guidelines for prehospital care — abstract not yet available (ahead-of-print), but this recurring review is the reference map of what guideline-level evidence exists in prehospital practice.
papers.relevance: 🔴 Low — Abstract not available and it's a guidelines roundup rather than a single adoptable intervention — flagged for the reading list.
papers.design: Biennial systematic review with NAM and AGREE II appraisal
papers.n: 71 prehospital evidence-based guidelines published 2023-2025
papers.finding: 52.1% (37/71) met all adapted NAM criteria for high quality; mean AGREE II overall score 70.9% (SD 11.4%); quality improved incrementally over prior reviews
papers.caveat: Review of guidelines only, not clinical outcomes; quality appraisal by design varies with tool
papers.shortTitle: 2026 review of prehospital guideline quality

papers.title: Documentation of Weight in Pediatric 9-1-1 Responses with Administration of Weight-Based Medications
papers.summary: Analysis of 57,378 US paediatric 9-1-1 responses where weight-based medications were given found 73.1% had a documented weight (or length-based estimate), with documentation less likely for adolescents (OR 0.87), Black patients (OR 0.72) and lower-acuity cases (OR 0.59), and more likely with advanced life support crews (OR 2.02).
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Weight-based paediatric dosing is core AP practice under the ACTAS CMGs, so the document-the-weight habit transfers — but this is a US documentation/QI study, so the numbers are local to their system.
papers.design: Retrospective national EMS database analysis
papers.n: 57,378 US paediatric 9-1-1 responses with weight-based medications
papers.finding: 73.1% (41,963) had documented weight or length-based estimate; less likely in adolescents (OR 0.87), Black patients (OR 0.72), lower acuity (OR 0.59); more likely with ALS crews (OR 2.02)
papers.caveat: US national dataset; documentation may not reflect actual weight assessment practice
papers.shortTitle: Paediatric weight often undocumented before dosing

papers.title: Consensus Guidelines for Prehospital Transfusion in Children: A Modified Delphi Study
papers.summary: Modified Delphi consensus guidelines for prehospital blood transfusion in children — abstract not yet available (ahead-of-print).
papers.relevance: 🔴 Low — No abstract yet, and blood products aren't in the extracted ACTAS formulary — would need a guideline change to adopt; worth noting QAS and other services run prehospital blood programs.
papers.design: Modified Delphi consensus study
papers.n: 20 multidisciplinary experts; 208 candidate items, 35 recommendations over six voting rounds
papers.finding: Consensus paediatric prehospital transfusion criteria: severe haemorrhage plus at least one shock indicator after first-line haemorrhage control, plus EMS clinical judgement; no consensus on EtCO2 as an indication
papers.caveat: Expert consensus with limited paediatric-specific evidence; prospective validation needed
papers.shortTitle: Consensus criteria for paediatric prehospital transfusion

papers.title: Mass casualty training for prehospital and emergency providers in Kigali, Rwanda: a quasi-experimental pre–post educational study
papers.summary: Quasi-experimental pre–post study of a two-part mass casualty training curriculum (asynchronous video modules plus a half-day simulation) for 41 emergency providers and community first responders in Kigali — mean knowledge scores rose significantly after training and remained above baseline at 3- and 6-month follow-up, with significant confidence gains across key MCI skills.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — the multimodal video-plus-simulation MCI training model transfers readily to Australian ambulance MCI preparedness, but this is a small pilot in an LMIC setting measuring knowledge and confidence, not patient or system outcomes.
papers.design: Quasi-experimental pre–post educational study
papers.n: 41 emergency providers and community first responders in Kigali, Rwanda
papers.finding: Mean knowledge scores rose significantly after training and remained above baseline at 3- and 6-month follow-up, with significant confidence gains across key MCI skills
papers.caveat: Small, single-centre pilot without control group; LMIC setting
papers.shortTitle: Kigali mass casualty training lifts knowledge

papers.title: Modelling eCPR eligibility after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a 10-year retrospective temporospatial analysis from a mixed urban-rural region in Germany
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: Ten-year German registry study modelling eCPR eligibility after OHCA in a mixed urban-rural region — of 1,696 analysed arrests, only 348 (20.5%) met local eligibility criteria at ambulance arrival and just 149 (8.8%) met the stricter modified ELSO definition, with the study also testing whether hypothetical intra-arrest transport strategies could meet a 60-minute low-flow target.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Directly maps to CMG 4/4A cardiac arrest care and the intra-arrest transport debate, but eCPR isn't an ACTAS capability — useful benchmark for OHCA system design rather than practice change
papers.design: Retrospective 10-year temporospatial registry cohort with hypothetical eCPR transport modelling
papers.n: 1,696 registry-documented OHCA cases (of 2,218) in Göttingen, Germany
papers.finding: 20.5% (348) met local eCPR criteria and 8.8% (149) modified ELSO criteria at EMS arrival; modelled on-scene eCPR gave median collapse-to-eCPR of 37 min (94.8% within 60 min) vs 75 min for intra-arrest transport (<1% within 60 min)
papers.caveat: Retrospective with hypothetical modelled scenarios; German mixed urban-rural system limits transferability
papers.shortTitle: Few OHCA patients eligible for eCPR in Germany

papers.title: Effectiveness of immersive virtual reality in undergraduate nursing students for cardiopulmonary resuscitation training: A randomized controlled trial
papers.summary: RCT of 246 undergraduate nursing students testing immersive VR plus manikin simulation against manikin simulation alone for CPR group training — no significant difference in self-confidence or CPR group performance after cluster adjustment, though students rated VR higher on satisfaction and usability, and 33.6% reported dizziness and 19% headaches from headsets.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Nursing-student education data, but directly relevant to ambulance service CPR training programs weighing up VR — the headline is hands-on sim alone did just as well
papers.design: Cluster-adjusted randomised controlled trial
papers.n: 246 undergraduate nursing students
papers.finding: No significant difference in self-confidence (adjusted effect 0.02, p=0.974) or CPR group performance (adjusted effect 0.56, p=0.153) with immersive VR plus manikin vs manikin alone; 33.6% reported dizziness and 19% headaches
papers.caveat: Nursing students in group CPR training, not practising paramedics; 19% adverse symptoms
papers.shortTitle: VR adds little to CPR simulation training

papers.title: When prehospital resuscitation attempts are unsuccessful: care for the relatives following termination of treatment in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: Interviews with 15 relatives present at unsuccessful out-of-hospital resuscitations showed their needs shift across three phases — dispatch guidance, help-or-withdraw during resus, then compassionate unhurried communication when efforts stop.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High transferability — death notification and family care are core AP work, directly actionable with no new kit
papers.design: Qualitative semi-structured interview study with systematic text condensation
papers.n: 15 relatives present at unsuccessful out-of-hospital resuscitations
papers.finding: Three phases with distinct needs: valued dispatch guidance, then either withdrawal or desire to assist during resuscitation, then compassionate unhurried communication at termination; community first responders provided emotional support.
papers.caveat: Small qualitative sample; Danish setting
papers.shortTitle: Relatives' needs after failed OHCA resuscitation

papers.title: Assessing accessibility to the extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation pathway for out-of-hospital cardiac arrests in London
papers.summary: Geospatial analysis of five years of London Ambulance Service OHCA data — of 776 patients meeting ECPR eligibility criteria, only 3% could reach an ECMO-capable centre within the 45-minute target, and stretching it to 60 minutes would lift access by 217%.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — no prehospital ECPR pathway in the ACT, but a sobering look at how eligibility on paper rarely equals access in practice
papers.design: Retrospective geospatial and pathway modelling study
papers.n: 776 ECPR-eligible OHCA patients over five years of London Ambulance Service data
papers.finding: Only 3% (23/776) were estimated to reach an ECMO-capable centre within 45 minutes during operating hours; extending the threshold to 60 minutes increased access by 217% (50 additional patients), with extending operating hours (+104%) and broader criteria (+52%) also helping.
papers.caveat: Modeled estimates from routine data in a single urban system
papers.shortTitle: Most ECPR-eligible London OHCAs can't reach ECMO in time

papers.title: Association between fentanyl use and mortality during prehospital emergency anaesthesia in traumatic brain injury – a retrospective cohort study
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: In 423 TBI patients intubated by a Finnish HEMS unit, fentanyl as an anaesthetic adjuvant was associated with lower mortality (OR 0.38), though selection bias can't be excluded.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — fentanyl is on the ACTAS formulary but prehospital anaesthesia is ICP-only, and the data is confounded
papers.design: Retrospective single-HEMS cohort with logistic regression
papers.n: 423 intubated TBI patients (353 fentanyl, 70 no fentanyl), single Finnish HEMS unit, 2014–2022
papers.finding: Fentanyl use was associated with lower mortality before discharge (OR 0.376, 95% CI 0.172–0.823, p=0.014); more post-intubation blood pressure decreases (48% vs 30% at 10% threshold) but fewer increases (18% vs 41%) in the fentanyl group.
papers.caveat: Substantial baseline differences suggest treatment selection bias may partly explain the finding
papers.shortTitle: Fentanyl in prehospital RSI for TBI linked to lower mortality

papers.title: Coronary angiography and reperfusion therapy following out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in women
papers.summary: Nationwide Swedish cohort of 8,641 post-OHCA admissions — women were less likely to undergo coronary angiography and PCI than men, yet intervention rates were even once angiographic findings were accounted for, and a third of angiographed women without shockable rhythm or ST elevation had significant coronary disease.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — in-hospital post-ROSC care, but a useful reminder that OHCA without ST elevation can still mean obstructive disease
papers.design: Nationwide registry cohort
papers.n: 8,641 patients admitted alive after OHCA (29.4% women)
papers.finding: Coronary angiography in 31.5% of women vs 51.0% of men; women less likely to undergo angiography (OR 0.77, 95% CI 0.66-0.90) and PCI (OR 0.76, 95% CI 0.64-0.90); after adjusting for angiographic findings intervention rates were similar (OR 0.97, 95% CI 0.80-1.18); significant coronary disease in 31% of angiographed women with non-shockable rhythm and no ST elevation
papers.caveat: Swedish registry data; residual confounding and no data on prehospital or out-of-hospital factors influencing angiography decisions
papers.shortTitle: Women post-OHCA get less angiography

papers.title: Access Block and Ambulance Ramping: The Canaries of the Healthcare System
papers.summary: A mixed-methods Queensland study of six years of ambulance and hospital records found access block is largely a hospital discharge ('back door') problem, with recommendations spanning discharge metrics, primary care support and prehospital flow.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High transferability — the best local evidence yet on what drives the ramping every crew experiences
papers.design: Mixed-methods study: umbrella review, qualitative interviews and quantitative analysis of six years of health system records
papers.n: 25 largest public hospitals in Queensland; patients and healthcare workers (numbers not reported)
papers.finding: Access block is largely a hospital discharge ('back door') problem; recommendations include inpatient discharge metrics, primary/community/aged care support, hospital-in-the-home alternatives, prehospital flow investment, extended-hour discharge lounges and funding reform
papers.caveat: Queensland-specific health system data; mixed-methods design not a controlled evaluation of interventions
papers.shortTitle: Ramping driven by hospital 'back door'

papers.title: Predicting the Prehospital Blood Transfusion Need in a Large Metropolitan Center
papers.summary: Retrospective cohort of 25,473 EMS-transported trauma patients in Los Angeles County — of those meeting prehospital blood transfusion criteria, 52% received blood within four hours, with SBP <90 mmHg and HR ≥110 bpm the best predictors of emergent transfusion.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — blood products aren't in the extracted ACTAS formulary (QAS, AV, SJWA and NSWA carry them)
papers.design: Retrospective observational cohort
papers.n: 25,473 EMS-transported trauma patients aged ≥15 in Los Angeles County; 905 met prehospital blood transfusion criteria
papers.finding: Of 905 patients meeting PHBT criteria, 475 (52%) received blood within four hours of ED arrival; SBP <90 mmHg and HR ≥110 bpm had the greatest positive predictive value for emergent transfusion
papers.caveat: Retrospective application of criteria before prehospital blood protocols existed; single-region US trauma system
papers.shortTitle: Predicting who needs prehospital blood

papers.title: Accuracy of ventilation feedback devices compared with a reference standard during asynchronous ventilation with continuous chest compressions in a simulated cardiac arrest: a prospective non-randomized cross-over study
papers.summary: Simulation cross-over study of two commercial ventilation feedback devices used during continuous compressions with asynchronous ventilations — both were clinically inaccurate, one displaying 111 breaths/min when the true rate was 12 and underestimating tidal volume by up to 440 mL in reversed airflow.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — cautionary tale for relying on feedback displays during asynchronous CPR
papers.design: Prospective, simulation-based, non-randomised cross-over study
papers.n: 20 emergency department nurse practitioners ventilating an intubated manikin (254 and 222 ventilations analysed)
papers.finding: EOLifeX® overestimated ventilation rate (111/min displayed vs 12/min true; bias +99 breaths/min) and underestimated tidal volume (104 mL vs 544 mL; bias -440 mL); AccuVent® displayed accurate rate but underestimated tidal volume (360 mL vs 532 mL; bias -172 mL)
papers.caveat: Manikin simulation with reversed airflow conditions; only two devices tested
papers.shortTitle: Ventilation feedback devices inaccurate during CPR

papers.title: Prognostic value of admission ionized calcium and acidosis in severely injured trauma patients
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: Multicentre trauma-registry cohort of 977 severely injured patients — admission hypocalcaemia was independently associated with hospital mortality and trauma-induced coagulopathy, while apparently elevated ionised calcium mostly reflected profound acidosis.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — no prehospital ionised calcium testing, but good context for calcium shifts during major-trauma resus
papers.design: Retrospective multicentre trauma registry cohort
papers.n: 977 adult trauma patients with admission ionised calcium (median ISS 25)
papers.finding: Hypocalcaemia (iCa²⁺ <1.10 mmol/L) in 291 (30%); independently associated with hospital mortality (OR 1.70, 95% CI 1.02-2.85) and trauma-induced coagulopathy (OR 2.24, 95% CI 1.58-3.18); apparent hypercalcaemia (8%) largely attributable to profound acidosis
papers.caveat: Retrospective design; single level-1 trauma centre dataset despite multicentre registry
papers.shortTitle: Admission hypocalcaemia predicts trauma mortality

papers.title: Temporal trends in chest compression quality during a metronome-guided CPR simulation: a secondary analysis of the RITMICO study
papers.summary: Secondary analysis of 477 volunteers in prolonged manikin CPR — compression depth and chest recoil decayed within minutes, and a double-click metronome with separate compression and release cues preserved quality significantly longer than a standard metronome.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — manikin study, but recoil decay is a real field problem and metronome cues are available on most defibrillators
papers.design: Secondary analysis of a simulation study (RITMICO) with linear mixed-effects modelling
papers.n: 477 volunteers performing prolonged manikin CPR
papers.finding: Compression depth and chest compression release velocity declined early during prolonged compressions; the double-click metronome produced consistently higher values for all CPR quality metrics than a standard metronome (all p<0.05) with later deterioration in release velocity
papers.caveat: Manikin simulation with volunteers, not real resuscitation; secondary analysis
papers.shortTitle: Double-click metronome preserves CPR quality

papers.title: Changes in LVOT velocity–time integral during whole blood donation: implications for early detection of hypovolemia in spontaneously breathing patients
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: Prospective study measuring LVOT VTI in 63 volunteers before and after donating about 6–7 mL/kg of blood — VTI fell 11.5% on average but with marked inter-individual variability, so it can't reliably flag mild hypovolaemia on its own.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — prehospital ultrasound isn't in the ACTAS skills corpus
papers.design: Prospective physiological study of volunteers before and after blood donation
papers.n: 63 healthy adult volunteers donating ~6-7 mL/kg blood
papers.finding: LVOT VTI fell 11.5% (95% CI -15.3 to -7.7) immediately after donation and remained 6.1% below baseline at 15 minutes; a ≥10% reduction occurred in only 50% (95% CI 37-63) of participants
papers.caveat: Healthy volunteers with controlled donation, not actual patients; marked inter-individual variability
papers.shortTitle: LVOT VTI unreliable for mild hypovolaemia

papers.title: The association of annual and daily volume with in-hospital mortality in Dutch and Danish Emergency Departments
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: Cohort of 724,256 ED presentations across Dutch and Danish hospitals — annual ED volume had no association with in-hospital mortality, while mortality was lower on busier days, driven by excess deaths on quiet ones.
papers.relevance: 🔴 Low transferability — in-hospital systems finding with no direct road application
papers.design: Retrospective international multicentre cohort with mixed-effects logistic regression
papers.n: 724,256 ED visits (486,558 Dutch, 237,698 Danish) across 12 EDs
papers.finding: Annual ED volume showed no association with in-hospital mortality; busier relative daily volume was associated with lower mortality in the Netherlands (e.g. dyspnoea AOR 0.89, 95% CI 0.86-0.92), driven by excess deaths on low-volume days
papers.caveat: Only 12 EDs in two European countries; adjusted observational associations cannot establish causation
papers.shortTitle: ED volume not linked to mortality

papers.title: Using Sydney Triage to Admission Risk Tool With Artificial Intelligence (START-AI) to Predict Inpatient Admitting Specialty for Emergency Department Patients: Single Centre Deep Learning Analysis
papers.summary: Sydney single-centre deep learning study of 40,054 admitted ED patients — a fine-tuned clinical language model predicted the inpatient admitting specialty from triage notes with AUROC 0.97, though precision was a moderate 0.71.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — ED-facing rather than prehospital, but shows where Australian AI triage is heading
papers.design: Single-centre deep learning analysis of electronic medical record data
papers.n: 40,054 admitted adult ED patients in Sydney
papers.finding: Bio-ClinicalBERT predicted one of 20 inpatient admitting teams with weighted AUROC 0.97 (95% CI 0.96-0.98), precision 0.71, accuracy 0.75 (0.88 when top two teams accepted)
papers.caveat: Single centre; moderate precision and only ~75% single-label accuracy; needs external validation
papers.shortTitle: AI predicts ED admitting team from triage notes

papers.title: Acute trauma alarms in Norway - a qualitative study of factors influencing primary care doctors’ decision to call out
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: Qualitative interview study of 20 Norwegian primary care doctors on how they decide whether to call out to acute trauma alarms from limited EMCC voice messages — despite the sparse information it remained a decisive factor, with experienced doctors using recognition-primed cues and weighing severity against travel distance and the risk of concurrent incidents.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Useful operational insight into call-out decisions under information scarcity, but it reflects Norway's doctor-response model rather than the ACTAS paramedic-first system
papers.design: Qualitative interview study with systematic text condensation
papers.n: 20 Norwegian primary care doctors
papers.finding: Five themes shaped call-out decisions: limited but sufficient information, severity versus distance, risk of concurrent incidents, professional responsibility, and competence/collaboration; experienced doctors used recognition-primed cues and heuristic intuition.
papers.caveat: Norwegian primary care doctor system; findings may not transfer to Australian paramedic models
papers.shortTitle: How GPs decide to respond to trauma alarms

papers.title: Discovery of eight stable subgroups of sepsis in the emergency department with consensus clustering
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: Retrospective consensus clustering of 953 ED sepsis admissions at Oslo University Hospital could not replicate the four SENECA phenotypes, instead finding eight stable subgroups with more granular characteristics — and only 49% of patients meeting SENECA inclusion criteria fulfilled Sepsis-3, underlining sepsis heterogeneity and cohort-definition problems.
papers.relevance: 🔴 Low — Retrospective ED phenotyping with no immediate prehospital application, though it reinforces why ACTAS sepsis recognition (CMG 38) leans on simple bedside criteria like qSOFA
papers.design: Retrospective consensus clustering cohort
papers.n: 953 adults with sepsis admitted to a single Oslo ED, 2019–2023
papers.finding: The four SENECA phenotypes could not be replicated; eight stable subgroups with more granular characteristics were identified. Only 49% of patients meeting SENECA inclusion criteria fulfilled Sepsis-3 criteria.
papers.caveat: Retrospective, single-centre data
papers.shortTitle: Eight sepsis subgroups found, SENECA not replicated

papers.title: Criteria for Safe Hospital Discharge in Bronchiolitis: A Systematic Review
papers.summary: Systematic review for the binational guideline update on discharge criteria for infants under 12 months with bronchiolitis — two retrospective studies (N=2,697) found structured discharge criteria significantly shortened length of stay with no difference in readmissions (low-to-very-low certainty), and informed the 2025 Australasian Bronchiolitis Guideline covering clinical stability, oxygen saturation/support, feeding, caregiver confidence, social factors and follow-up.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — hospital ED/inpatient decision-making rather than on-road practice, but directly Australasian and shapes the pathway for infants we transport
papers.design: Systematic review informing guideline update
papers.n: Two retrospective observational studies, 2,697 infants under 12 months with bronchiolitis
papers.finding: Both studies found structured discharge criteria significantly reduced length of stay with no significant difference in readmission rates; evidence certainty low to very low. Informed the 2025 Australasian Bronchiolitis Guideline discharge criteria.
papers.caveat: Only two retrospective studies with low to very low certainty evidence
papers.shortTitle: Bronchiolitis discharge criteria cut length of stay

papers.title: Evaluating the effect of a regional training initiative on bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation rates after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest
papers.summary: Difference-in-differences evaluation of a year-long community hands-only CPR training initiative across 20,414 OHCAs — overall bystander CPR rates rose from 37.4% to 42.5% but the adjusted intervention effect wasn't significant (+2.94 pp, 95% CI −0.95 to 6.83); only public-location arrests showed a significant increase (+8.59 pp), with no effect at home and no detectable survival or neurological benefit.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Bystander CPR education underpins Australian community resuscitation strategy and ambulance-led CPR awareness campaigns — the public-but-not-home signal is directly relevant to how we target training effort.
papers.design: Difference-in-differences registry evaluation (CARES, 2022–2024)
papers.n: 20,414 OHCA patients (15,417 intervention region)
papers.finding: Overall bystander CPR rose 37.4% to 42.5% but adjusted intervention effect not significant (+2.94 pp, 95% CI −0.95 to 6.83); public-location arrests +8.59 pp (95% CI 0.22–16.96); no significant effect at home or on survival or neurologically intact survival
papers.caveat: Non-randomised county comparison; possible secular trends and contamination
papers.shortTitle: Community CPR training only helps public arrests

papers.title: Transoesophageal echocardiography during cardiopulmonary resuscitation for cardiac arrest: a scoping review
papers.summary: Scoping review of 22 studies (1,254 patients, 84% OHCA) mapping intra-arrest transoesophageal echocardiography — insertion succeeded in 80–100% of cases and TEE changed management in 31–48% of patients, but the two randomised trials found no difference in ROSC, survival, or favourable neurological outcome versus conventional CPR.
papers.relevance: 🔴 Low — TEE is an in-hospital, physician-level tool with no prehospital role in ACTAS — interesting for where resuscitation science is heading, but nothing changes on the road, and no patient-centred benefit has been shown.
papers.design: Scoping review of 22 studies
papers.n: 1,254 patients (84% OHCA)
papers.finding: Successful TEE insertion 80–100%; TEE changed management in 31–48%; two RCTs found no difference in ROSC, survival or favourable neurological outcome versus conventional CPR
papers.caveat: Mostly single-centre observational studies without comparators; no long-term outcome data
papers.shortTitle: Intra-arrest TOE feasible but no survival gain

papers.title: Prehospital emergency cricothyroidotomy in Denmark: a nationwide cohort study, 2016–2023
papers.summary: Nationwide Danish cohort of all 71 prehospital emergency cricothyroidotomies over 2016–2023 — overall procedural success 87.3% (83.3% in OHCA), aspiration and oropharyngeal bleeding the commonest indications, but the procedure was rare (0.12% of 39,885 OHCAs) and OHCA outcomes were poor (ROSC 25%, 30-day survival 4.5%, 1-year survival 2.3%).
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A failed-airway rescue skill relevant to ACTAS but ICP-only (CMG 3B intubation algorithm incl. surgical airway), and the data come from a physician-staffed system, so case mix and operator context differ from ours.
papers.design: Nationwide registry-based observational cohort
papers.n: 71 patients undergoing prehospital emergency cricothyroidotomy (48 with OHCA), Denmark 2016–2023
papers.finding: Procedural success 87.3% overall (83.3% in OHCA, 95.7% non-OHCA). Cricothyroidotomy performed in 48 of 39,885 OHCAs (0.12%). In OHCA patients, ROSC 25.0%, 30-day survival 4.5%, one-year survival 2.3%.
papers.caveat: Registry-based design in a physician-staffed Danish EMS system; very small numbers limit generalisability
papers.shortTitle: Prehospital cricothyroidotomy: rare but often successful

papers.title: Ultrasound Archiving in the Emergency Department: Implementation, Governance and 4‐Year Outcomes at an Australian Tertiary Emergency Department
papers.summary: Four-year implementation study of a middleware ED ultrasound archiving and QA workflow at Nepean Hospital — 7,281 studies archived across 15 modalities with zero data loss or failures, automated trainee logbooks saving each trainee ~2 h/week, and clinician time (not software) the dominant recurring cost.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — ED-based governance, not prehospital, but the archiving/QA/logbook template is directly relevant to any Australian ambulance service building an ultrasound QA or training program.
papers.design: Single-centre retrospective service implementation analysis
papers.n: 7,281 archived ED ultrasound studies across 15 modalities at one Australian tertiary ED
papers.finding: No failures or data loss over four years; annual volume grew from 1,083 (2022) to 2,224 (2025); automated trainee logbooks save each trainee ~2 hours/week; dominant recurring cost was clinician time.
papers.caveat: Single-centre retrospective implementation report without comparison group
papers.shortTitle: ED ultrasound archiving works in Australia

papers.title: Racial and ethnic differences in bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation for opioid-associated out-of-hospital cardiac arrests
papers.summary: Retrospective cohort study using NEMSIS data (n=19,612) found Black patients with opioid-associated OHCA had significantly lower odds of receiving bystander CPR than White patients (AOR 0.70, 95% CI 0.63-0.77), with Hispanic patients also less likely (AOR 0.82).
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — US-specific dataset and racial categories, but core message about bCPR disparities in opioid-associated arrests is relevant to Australian public health messaging and overdose response awareness.
papers.design: Retrospective national registry cohort (NEMSIS 2017–2025)
papers.n: 19,612 EMS-assessed opioid-associated OHCAs in adults
papers.finding: Compared with White patients, Black patients had lower odds of bystander CPR (AOR 0.70, 95% CI 0.63–0.77); Hispanic patients also lower (AOR 0.82)
papers.caveat: Registry data limited adjustment; US system may not generalise to Australia
papers.shortTitle: Racial gaps in bystander CPR for opioid OHCA

papers.title: RhD-Positive Transfusion in Females of Childbearing Potential in Hemorrhagic Shock: Risk, Reality, and Policy
papers.summary: Narrative review synthesising evidence on D-alloimmunization and HDFN risk found modeling studies estimate fetal death due to anti-D-mediated HDFN would occur in fewer than 0.1% of females of childbearing potential exposed to RhD-positive blood products in trauma, supporting prehospital RhD-positive transfusion when RhD-negative unavailable.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Directly relevant to haemorrhagic shock management but ACTAS does not carry blood products — would require guideline change and formulary expansion to adopt.
papers.design: Narrative review
papers.n: Not reported
papers.finding: Modelling studies estimate fetal death from anti-D-mediated HDFN in fewer than 0.1% of females of childbearing potential exposed to RhD-positive blood products in trauma, supporting RhD-positive transfusion when RhD-negative products unavailable
papers.caveat: Narrative review reliant largely on modelling studies rather than direct outcome data
papers.shortTitle: RhD-positive prehospital blood OK for women

papers.title: Potential Risks With the SPEAR®, a New Device Marketed for Out-of-Hospital Needle Decompression of the Chest
papers.summary: Safety warning about potential risks with the SPEAR® device marketed for out-of-hospital needle decompression of the chest. Abstract not yet available (ahead-of-print).
papers.relevance: 🔴 Low — ACTAS does not use SPEAR for needle decompression, but safety alerts on new devices are worth noting even if we don't carry the equipment
papers.shortTitle: Safety warning: SPEAR chest decompression device

papers.title: Effect of Body Position on Chest Compression Quality During CPR in an Obesity Simulation Model: A Randomized Crossover Trial
papers.summary: Randomised crossover simulation trial testing whether 10cm elevation of paramedics improves chest compression quality in obese manikins — it didn't, obesity still impaired compression depth by ~18mm despite increased rescuer effort
papers.relevance: 🟢 High transferability — Directly relevant to cardiac arrest care (CMG 4), practical ergonomic finding that doesn't require equipment change
papers.design: Randomised crossover simulation trial
papers.n: 60 paramedics
papers.finding: Compression depth reduced ~18 mm with simulated obesity (adjusted mean differences 17.83 mm and 18.44 mm vs standard, both p<0.001); 10 cm paramedic elevation made no difference (p=0.523)
papers.caveat: Simulation with manikins, not real patients
papers.shortTitle: Paramedic elevation doesn't help CPR in obesity simulation

papers.title: Prehospital Blood Transfusion for Medical Causes of Hemorrhage: A Case Series
papers.summary: Retrospective observational study of prehospital whole blood for non-traumatic haemorrhagic shock across two US systems — GI bleeding (49%) and unspecified shock (43%) were the main indications, vitals improved (HR 102→96, SBP 83→106)
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — Not in the ACTAS formulary — blood products are not carried, would require guideline change to adopt
papers.design: Retrospective observational study across two fire-based EMS systems
papers.n: 47 patients given prehospital blood for non-traumatic haemorrhagic shock
papers.finding: Of 163 transfusions, 50 (30.7%) were non-traumatic; GI bleeding 49%, unspecified shock 43%; mean HR fell 102→96, SBP rose 83→106 mmHg, shock index 1.34→1.01
papers.caveat: Small case series without outcome or control data; US fire-based systems
papers.shortTitle: Prehospital blood for non-traumatic haemorrhage

papers.title: Between Hemorrhage and Harm: Complications of the Abdominal Aortic and Junctional Tourniquet-Stabilized
papers.summary: Case report of a patient with AAJT-S placed prehospital for pelvic gunshot wounds who suffered cardiac arrest upon device removal and developed metabolic acidosis, compartment syndrome, rhabdomyolysis, renal and liver infarcts, pulmonary emboli, and stroke
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — Cautionary finding for junctional tourniquet use — AAJT-S isn't specified as ACTAS equipment, but principles apply to non-compressible torso haemorrhage management
papers.design: Case report with literature review
papers.n: 1 young adult male with pelvic and lower limb gunshot wounds
papers.finding: Removal of a prehospital AAJT-S was followed by cardiac arrest and complications including metabolic acidosis, compartment syndrome, rhabdomyolysis, renal and liver infarcts, pulmonary emboli and stroke
papers.caveat: Single case; confounding by injury severity and shock cannot be excluded
papers.shortTitle: Junctional tourniquet harm after pelvic GSW

papers.title: Rate of future hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn following the prehospital transfusion of RhD-positive blood products to females of childbearing potential in the United States of America
papers.summary: In silico simulation modelling future haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn risk in 957 US females of childbearing potential who received prehospital RhD-positive blood — annual HDFN risk ranged 0.214–0.294% across regions
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — Not in the ACTAS formulary — blood products are not carried, but important safety consideration if ACTAS ever adopts prehospital blood
papers.design: In silico simulation modelling
papers.n: 957 US females of childbearing potential transfused prehospital with RhD-positive products over ~5 years; 19.5 million simulated FCPs
papers.finding: Annual future HDFN risk ranged 0.214% (Northeast) to 0.294% (South); 1,368 cases over the 2,500-year simulation (0.55/year), i.e. one case every ~2.4–80.7 years by region
papers.caveat: Modelled estimates reliant on assumptions about nativity, age distribution and future pregnancy rates
papers.shortTitle: Low HDFN risk after prehospital RhD-positive blood

papers.title: Population-based implementation of a mobile emergency medical service platform in Hiroshima, Japan
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: Population-based descriptive study of a Japanese mobile EMS app capturing 147,213 transport cases over 15 months — 90% were emergency transports, OCR used in 74% of cases, hospital acceptance on first request in 66% with median 5.2 min negotiation time
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — Operational innovation relevant to digitising prehospital data and hospital coordination, but Japanese system context differs from ACTAS
papers.design: Population-based descriptive study of a mobile EMS application
papers.n: 147,213 EMS transport cases in Hiroshima Prefecture over 15 months
papers.finding: 90% were emergency transports; hospital acceptance on first request in 66% with median negotiation time 5.2 min; OCR used in 74% of cases; 1,988 cardiac arrest cases captured
papers.caveat: Descriptive, single prefecture in a different EMS system; no outcome impact assessed
papers.shortTitle: Japanese mobile EMS app rollout data

papers.title: Public Acceptance, Trust, and Self-Efficacy Related to Drone-Assisted Emergency Medical Response in Louisiana
papers.summary: Cross-sectional survey of 586 Louisiana adults on drone-assisted emergency response — high acceptance (mean 4.1/5), trust (3.8), and self-efficacy (4.0), with telecommunicator guidance significantly increasing self-efficacy for both family and stranger scenarios
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — Forward-looking innovation relevant to future service models, but ACTAS doesn't currently use drones for medical delivery
papers.design: Cross-sectional online survey
papers.n: 586 Louisiana adults
papers.finding: Mean acceptance 4.1/5, trust 3.8/5, self-efficacy 4.0/5; trust and self-efficacy strongest predictors of acceptance (R²=.57); telecommunicator guidance increased self-efficacy (Cohen's d 0.41–0.44)
papers.caveat: Single US state, online panel sample; attitudes may not predict real-world use
papers.shortTitle: Public accepts drone-delivered AEDs

papers.title: Blunt versus penetrating trauma: differences in early physiology, coagulopathy, and outcomes in a Scandinavian trauma centre
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: This Swedish registry of 2,193 trauma patients (353 penetrating) found penetrating trauma patients were younger (median 34 vs 49 years), more often male (78% vs 66%), more frequently in shock on arrival (5.9% vs 2.2%), and more likely to require emergency surgery (53% vs 30%) and early blood transfusion (20% vs 4.5%).
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — CMG 14 Shock and CMG 39 Major Trauma are relevant AP scope, but the paper focuses heavily on blood products (not carried by ACTAS) and hospital-based outcomes — early shock recognition is useful, transfusion findings don't translate
papers.design: Registry-based observational cohort study
papers.n: 2,193 adult trauma patients (353 penetrating)
papers.finding: Penetrating trauma patients more often in shock (5.9% vs 2.2%), more emergency surgery (53% vs 30%) and early transfusion (20% vs 4.5%); blunt trauma had higher ISS (median 10 vs 4) and worse functional outcomes; 30-day mortality not significantly different after adjustment
papers.caveat: Single Scandinavian trauma centre; not generalisable to Australian prehospital systems
papers.shortTitle: Blunt vs penetrating trauma physiology and outcomes

papers.title: Practice variability of epinephrine administration in pediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in the United States
papers.summary: Retrospective analysis of US NEMSIS data found adrenaline was administered in only 60% of paediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrests, with longer scene times, advanced airway attempts, and defibrillation associated with higher odds of administration, while public settings and female sex correlated with lower odds.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Adrenaline is carried by ACTAS (AP scope) and paediatric cardiac arrest is within our scope—US practice patterns are directly relevant despite jurisdictional differences.
papers.design: Retrospective observational analysis of US NEMSIS 2021 registry data
papers.n: 8,495 paediatric OHCA events managed by ALS units
papers.finding: 40.2% of paediatric OHCA events received no adrenaline; administration associated with younger age, urban setting, scene time >10 min, advanced airway attempt (OR 8.33) and defibrillation (OR 1.95); lower odds in public settings (OR 0.55) and females (OR 0.83)
papers.caveat: Registry data reliant on documentation accuracy; associations do not establish causation
papers.shortTitle: Adrenaline given in only 60% of paediatric OHCA

papers.title: Predicting Prehospital Blood Transfusion After Motor Vehicle Trauma
papers.summary: Machine learning models using NEMSIS data achieved strong discrimination (AUC 0.906) for predicting prehospital blood transfusion after motor vehicle trauma, identifying physiologic measures and shock designation as key predictors.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Predictive models and epidemiology are relevant for trauma service planning, but blood products are not carried by ACTAS—would require guideline/infrastructure change to implement.
papers.design: Retrospective registry cohort with machine learning (NEMSIS)
papers.n: 2,078,452 EMS activations for MVC; derivation cohort 303,383
papers.finding: Ridge-selected model AUC 0.942 (sensitivity 63.9%, specificity 97.7%); random forest-selected model AUC 0.901; physiologic composites and shock designation were key predictors; ~3.4–3.6% of national cohort predicted high probability of prehospital blood transfusion
papers.caveat: US registry data; models predict transfusion given rather than true need, and derivation from agencies already running blood programs may bias predictors
papers.shortTitle: Predicting prehospital blood need after MVC trauma

papers.title: Diagnostic accuracy, characteristics and survival of children with trauma in HEMS: a retrospective multi-centre observational study
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: Multi-centre Swiss HEMS study of 282 paediatric trauma patients found moderate diagnostic accuracy between prehospital and in-hospital diagnoses (Cohen's κ=0.64), with polytrauma underdiagnosed and extremity/pelvic injuries overdiagnosed, and overall survival of 92.2%.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Paediatric trauma management is within ACTAS scope (CMG 39 Major Trauma), but this is physician-staffed HEMS—diagnostic patterns and survival benchmarks are useful context despite model differences.
papers.design: Retrospective multi-centre observational study
papers.n: 282 paediatric trauma patients (≤16 years) transported by Swiss HEMS
papers.finding: Cohen's κ between prehospital and in-hospital diagnoses 0.64 (95% CI 0.58–0.70); polytrauma underdiagnosed, extremity/pelvic injuries overdiagnosed; survival to discharge and 1 year 92.2%
papers.caveat: Physician-staffed HEMS system with few paediatric missions; not directly comparable to paramedic-staffed systems; heterogeneous vital signs documentation
papers.shortTitle: Paediatric trauma diagnosis accuracy in Swiss HEMS

papers.title: Feasibility and Acceptability of Mobilizing Community Paramedics to Provide the Standard of Care for Pediatric Concussion: Mobile Integrated Health Programming for Pediatric Patients
papers.summary: Experimental mixed-methods study demonstrated that a Mobile Integrated Health program using community paramedics for paediatric concussion follow-up was feasible and acceptable, with 19% patient enrolment and improvement in Post-Concussion Symptoms Scale scores.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — MIH and community paramedic models are conceptually relevant to Australian services, though ACTAS doesn't have a formal CP tier—the feasibility and satisfaction data inform potential program development.
papers.design: Experimental mixed-methods feasibility study
papers.n: 15 community paramedics; 30 of 156 eligible patients enrolled
papers.finding: 19% (30/156) enrolment; 28 home visits completed; PCSS improved from mean 15.2 pre-visit to 8.8 post-visit (p<0.05); high satisfaction (patients/parents mean 4.4/5, CPs 4.0/5)
papers.caveat: Small, uncontrolled feasibility study with no clinical outcome comparison
papers.shortTitle: Community paramedics for paediatric concussion follow-up

papers.title: Indirect ICU Admissions From an Australian Emergency Department: Risk Factors and Outcomes
papers.summary: Australian observational study found indirect ICU admissions (ED admission to non-critical care ward requiring ICU transfer within 24 hours) accounted for 11.3% of ED-to-ICU admissions, with circulatory insufficiency as the most common reason and hospital mortality of 12.8%.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Australian study directly relevant to local practice—indirect ICU admissions reflect missed deterioration recognition after handover, which has implications for paramedic documentation and communication.
papers.design: Observational cohort study
papers.n: 148 indirect ICU admissions at one Australian hospital
papers.finding: 11.3% of ED-to-ICU admissions were indirect; circulatory insufficiency most common (43%); 53% had normal observations; hospital mortality 12.8%
papers.caveat: Single-centre, in-hospital ED cohort with small sample
papers.shortTitle: Indirect ICU admissions from Australian ED

papers.title: Distribution of clinically identified reversible causes in emergency department and out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a retrospective cohort study
papers.summary: Retrospective cohort study comparing reversible causes in ED vs. out-of-hospital cardiac arrest — hypoxia was the most common cause overall but occurred less frequently in ED arrests (46.6% vs 57.2%), while hypovolemia (33.1% vs 23.2%) and cardiac tamponade (2.9% vs 0.6%) were significantly more common in ED.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Directly applicable to cardiac arrest resuscitation (CMG 4) — reinforces the 5Hs and 5Ts framework and shows ED arrests have a different cause profile that may inform transport decisions and pre-arrival preparation.
papers.design: Retrospective cohort, single tertiary ED, 2018-2024
papers.n: 910 adults in cardiac arrest (275 ED, 635 OHCA)
papers.finding: Hypoxia less frequent in ED arrest (46.6% vs 57.2%; aOR 0.61), hypovolaemia (33.1% vs 23.2%; aOR 1.80) and tamponade (2.9% vs 0.6%; aOR 5.14) more frequent in ED arrest
papers.caveat: Single centre; clinically identified/suspected causes, not definitive aetiologies
papers.shortTitle: Reversible causes: ED vs out-of-hospital arrest

papers.title: Feasibility and acceptability of pediatric expert teleconsultation during critical ambulance transports: a pilot randomized controlled simulation trial
papers.summary: Simulated RCT testing teleconsultation for paediatric ambulance transports — paramedics found it acceptable (TUS 5.8/7) and experienced less frustration (p=0.03) with 94% attempting physician contact, though physicians reported higher workload (p=0.01) and 92% connected in ≤2 attempts.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Operational innovation with potential relevance to regional/remote paediatric retrievals, but requires significant technology infrastructure and physician on-call availability — Australian implementation would need local validation.
papers.design: Pilot randomised controlled simulation trial with mixed methods
papers.n: 24 paramedic-physician teams (12 per group), 72 simulated paediatric transports
papers.finding: Paramedic acceptability high (TUS 5.8/7); physician contact attempted in 94% of transports (vs 47% control), 92% connected in ≤2 attempts; paramedic workload similar but less frustration (p=0.03); physician workload higher (p=0.01)
papers.caveat: Simulation setting; outcomes do not reflect real-world patients or technical reliability
papers.shortTitle: Paediatric teleconsultation during ambulance transport

papers.title: Intramuscular midazolam versus intravenous clonazepam for prehospital treatment of generalized tonic-clonic seizures: A randomized double-blind non-inferiority trial
papers.summary: Randomised double-blind non-inferiority trial testing whether IM midazolam is non-inferior to IV clonazepam for prehospital seizures — it was, with 75% treatment success for IM midazolam versus 62.5% for IV clonazepam (risk difference +12.5 percentage points; 95% CI -10.0 to +33.4).
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Directly relevant to prehospital seizure management — IM midazolam is widely used in Australia and this RCT supports its use when IV access would delay treatment.
papers.design: Randomised double-blind non-inferiority trial (physician-staffed EMS, Tunis)
papers.n: 64 patients aged ≥14 with witnessed tonic-clonic seizures ≥5 min (32 per group)
papers.finding: Treatment success 75% IM midazolam vs 62.5% IV clonazepam (risk difference +12.5 pp; 95% CI -10.0 to +33.4), meeting non-inferiority; time to seizure cessation shorter with IM midazolam (1:42 vs 3:13 min)
papers.caveat: Small sample; wide confidence interval; physician-staffed Tunisian system may not generalise
papers.shortTitle: IM midazolam non-inferior for prehospital seizures

papers.title: Wearable saving lives: a case report
papers.summary: Case report demonstrating that smartwatch fall detection can serve as a digital witness in unwitnessed out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, triggering alerts that enabled timely CPR initiation and resulted in favourable neurological recovery.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Commercial wearable technology is widely available in the community, and EMS personnel increasingly encounter patients with smartwatches triggering alerts — understanding this workflow improves response coordination and outcomes.
papers.design: Case report
papers.n: 1 man, 69, with unwitnessed OHCA while running
papers.finding: Smartwatch fall detection triggered automated alerts; CPR started ~6-7 min after collapse; VF was initial rhythm, ROSC achieved, discharged day 29 with complete neurological recovery
papers.caveat: Single case; no evidence of generalisable benefit
papers.shortTitle: Smartwatch fall detection witnesses OHCA

papers.title: Workplace violence from the ambulance personnel's perspective, a qualitative study
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: Qualitative study with Swedish ambulance personnel identified three themes driving workplace violence: personnel lack of competence and willingness to adapt, inability to cope with emotional responses to provocation, and limited control in unpredictable situations involving intoxicated or unpredictable patients.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Swedish ambulance service context differs from Australian models in staffing, scope of practice, and patient demographics, though the themes of situational control and emotional coping translate broadly to prehospital work.
papers.design: Qualitative focus group study with reflexive thematic analysis
papers.n: 10 Swedish ambulance personnel in 3 focus groups
papers.finding: Three themes: personnel lack of competence/willingness to adapt, inability to cope with emotional responses to provocation, and limited control in unpredictable situations (e.g. intoxicated patients)
papers.caveat: Small Swedish sample of personnel who personally experienced violence; findings may not transfer to Australian systems
papers.shortTitle: Why ambulance workplace violence occurs

papers.title: Health inequalities in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest incidence and bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation rates in England 2018–23
papers.summary: Retrospective analysis of 165,701 OHCA patients in England 2018–23 found 23.6% of postcode districts remain high-risk (higher OHCA incidence, lower bystander CPR rates), with urban deprived areas showing 71.2% BCPR versus 79.1% in low-risk areas, though ROSC and survival were slightly higher in high-risk areas.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — OHCA epidemiology and CPR inequality — findings generalizable to Australian contexts with socioeconomic disparities
papers.design: Retrospective geospatial registry analysis
papers.n: 165,701 OHCA patients across 2,102 postcode districts
papers.finding: 499 high-risk postcode districts (23.6%) with higher OHCA incidence and lower bystander CPR (71.2% vs 79.1% in low-risk areas); ROSC (27.4% vs 26.5%) and survival (8.2% vs 7.9%) slightly higher in high-risk areas; patterns unchanged since 2013-2015.
papers.caveat: English data and registry-based, so findings may not generalise to the Australian context
papers.shortTitle: Persistent OHCA inequality across England

papers.title: Emergency Medical Services Equipment Use in the Emergency Department and Time to Care for Those With Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
papers.summary: Video review study of 223 OHCA patients found using EMS equipment for initial ED rhythm analysis reduced median time to first rhythm analysis by 143 seconds and first defibrillation by 131.5 seconds compared with ED equipment.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Operational protocol with direct application to Australian practice — we often transfer OHCA patients with our defibrillators attached
papers.design: Single-centre retrospective video review
papers.n: 223 adults with OHCA
papers.finding: Initial ED rhythm analysis with EMS equipment shortened median time to first ED rhythm analysis by 143 seconds (95% CI 116–169) and first ED defibrillation by 131.5 seconds (95% CI 8–272); 8 patients survived to discharge
papers.caveat: Single-centre retrospective video review with non-randomised groups and different baseline rhythm distributions
papers.shortTitle: Using EMS gear speeds ED rhythm analysis

papers.title: Prognostic performance of plasma and urinary biomarkers of kidney injury and function after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest
papers.summary: Prospective study of 82 comatose OHCA patients found kidney-specific biomarkers (plasma and urinary NGAL and KIM-1, cystatin C) were superior to serum creatinine for early AKI detection and prediction of poor neurological outcomes at discharge.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Hospital-based biomarker research — relevant for post-arrest care but not prehospital decision-making
papers.design: Prospective observational biomarker study
papers.n: 82 comatose adults with OHCA
papers.finding: Kidney-specific biomarkers (plasma and urinary NGAL, KIM-1, cystatin C) outperformed serum creatinine for early AKI detection and predicting poor neurological outcome; AKI in 65.9%, CPC 3–5 in 54.9%
papers.caveat: Small single-cohort observational study; biomarkers measured post-ROSC, limited relevance to prehospital care
papers.shortTitle: Kidney biomarkers predict outcomes after OHCA

papers.title: Association of serum lactate with outcome after pediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a secondary analysis of the Therapeutic Hypothermia After Pediatric Cardiac Arrest (THAPCA) trial
papers.summary: Secondary analysis of 213 pediatric OHCA patients found higher lactate within 6 hours of ROSC was associated with unfavorable 12-month neurobehavioral outcomes (median 7.8 vs 3.1 mmol/L), with each 1 mmol/L increase increasing odds of unfavorable outcome by 40%.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Pediatric OHCA prognostication — limited direct prehospital application but valuable for understanding long-term outcomes
papers.design: Secondary analysis of the THAPCA-OH randomised trial
papers.n: 213 children with OHCA
papers.finding: Median first lactate within 6 h of ROSC was 7.8 vs 3.1 mmol/L for unfavourable vs favourable 12-month outcome; each 1 mmol/L increase raised odds of unfavourable outcome 1.40-fold (95% CI 1.17–1.69)
papers.caveat: Secondary analysis of trial population; association, not validated as a prognostic tool
papers.shortTitle: Lactate after paediatric OHCA predicts outcome

papers.title: Association between preexisting electrocardiographic abnormalities and shockable initial rhythm in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest
papers.summary: Danish registry study of 22,516 first OHCA patients found prehospital ECG abnormalities (pathological Q-waves, LVH, AF, conduction delays, LBBB) were associated with higher odds of shockable initial rhythm in bystander-witnessed arrests.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Retrospective hospital-based analysis — predictive value of historical ECGs but not actionable at roadside
papers.design: National registry cohort with linked prior ECGs
papers.n: 22,516 people with first OHCA (Denmark)
papers.finding: In bystander-witnessed arrests, prior ECG abnormalities were associated with higher odds of shockable initial rhythm (any abnormality OR 1.44, 95% CI 1.10–1.90; LBBB OR 2.03, 95% CI 1.49–2.77; AF OR 1.70, 95% CI 1.38–2.10)
papers.caveat: Only 38.7% of witnessed arrests had a prior ECG available, potential selection bias
papers.shortTitle: Prior ECG abnormalities predict shockable OHCA rhythm

papers.title: Intravenous Magnesium Sulfate for Acute Nontraumatic Headache in the Emergency Department
papers.summary: RCT of 1,028 ED patients with acute nontraumatic headache found IV magnesium sulfate plus paracetamol achieved more frequent treatment success (78.9% vs 65.1%) but pain score differences were below clinical importance thresholds, with less rescue analgesia needed but more mild side effects.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — ED-based analgesia trial — magnesium showed statistical but not clinically meaningful benefit for prehospital use
papers.design: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial
papers.n: 1,028 adults with acute nontraumatic headache
papers.finding: MgSO4 plus paracetamol: treatment success 78.9% vs 65.1% (difference 13.8%, 95% CI 8–19), but pain score differences below 1.3-point clinical importance threshold; less rescue analgesia (7.1% vs 15.3%) and more adverse events (15.4% vs 11.1%)
papers.caveat: Benefits below accepted thresholds for clinical importance; ED-based, single-centre
papers.shortTitle: IV magnesium adds little for ED headache

papers.title: MRI-based quantitative profiling of hypoxic-ischemic brain injury in postanoxic status epilepticus and other EEG patterns
papers.summary: Two-center study of 192 postanoxic patients using quantitative MRI found postanoxic status epilepticus exhibited more favorable hypoxic-ischemic brain injury profiles (higher whole-brain ADC values) compared with generalized periodic discharges or malignant EEG patterns.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Advanced neuroprognostication research — hospital-based MRI study not applicable to prehospital care
papers.design: Retrospective two-centre observational study with quantitative MRI
papers.n: 192 comatose post-cardiac arrest patients
papers.finding: Whole-brain ADC values were lower in malignant patterns and GPDs (838 × 10⁻⁶ mm²/s) than in postanoxic status epilepticus (893 × 10⁻⁶ mm²/s) and benign patterns (907 × 10⁻⁶ mm²/s); 30.7% recovered from coma
papers.caveat: Retrospective, in-hospital ICU population, no outcome effect confirmed
papers.shortTitle: MRI profiles of postanoxic status epilepticus

papers.title: Identifying Quality Indicators for Prehospital Care Following Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Focused Scoping Review
papers.summary: Scoping review identified 16 potential quality indicators for prehospital post-ROSC care across five domains, highlighting a major evidence gap since only two existing studies listed formal indicators.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High transferability — Directly addresses prehospital practice gap — quality indicators could standardise post-ROSC care and benchmark performance
papers.design: Focused scoping review (PRISMA-guided)
papers.n: 46 studies included from 337 records
papers.finding: Only 2 included studies listed formal quality indicators; 16 potential prehospital post-ROSC quality indicators were extracted across five domains
papers.caveat: Most included studies were in-hospital; scoping review without formal consensus yet
papers.shortTitle: Few quality indicators for prehospital post-ROSC care

papers.title: PRECEPT-OHCA: prehospital evaluation of confidence and practice in the treatment of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest across Australia, the United Kingdom, and New Zealand: a cross-sectional study protocol
papers.summary: Cross-sectional survey protocol will assess paramedic confidence in identifying OHCA reversible causes across Australia, UK and New Zealand, evaluating equipment availability and perceived barriers.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High transferability — Australian context with direct relevance to paramedic practice — findings could inform training and equipment decisions
papers.design: International cross-sectional survey protocol
papers.n: Not reported (≥382 responses targeted)
papers.shortTitle: Survey protocol: paramedic OHCA reversible causes

papers.title: Whole Blood Versus Component Therapy for Out-of-Hospital Trauma Resuscitation
papers.summary: Review compared whole blood versus component therapy for out-of-hospital trauma resuscitation — direct clinical relevance for prehospital blood product protocols.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High transferability — Directly addresses a key prehospital clinical question — blood product selection affects trauma resuscitation protocols
papers.shortTitle: Whole blood vs components in prehospital trauma

papers.title: Research and Knowledge Translation Priorities for the Prehospital Care of Older Adults: A Modified Delphi Study
papers.summary: Modified Delphi study identified five high-priority research themes for older adult prehospital care, with falls assessment, prevention, and clinician training ranking highest across research and knowledge translation domains.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High transferability — Older adults represent growing EMS demographic — findings should guide research and practice priorities for this population
papers.design: Modified Delphi study with multidisciplinary stakeholder panel
papers.n: 28 stakeholders (EMS clinicians, geriatricians, medical directors, educators and others)
papers.finding: 145 candidate priorities consolidated into 30 themes; 17 advanced to final ranking; five high-priority, high-consensus topics identified in both research and knowledge translation domains, four shared, centring on assessment after perceived low-acuity falls, fall prevention, clinician training, and assessment tools
papers.caveat: Consensus priorities reflect stakeholder opinion, not evidence of effect, and likely reflect the participating health system
papers.shortTitle: Research priorities for prehospital older adult care

papers.title: Device safety during dual defibrillation requires implementation frameworks, not just post-use testing
papers.summary: Commentary argued dual defibrillation safety requires implementation frameworks and training protocols, not just post-use device testing, due to risks of electrical arcing and device damage.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High transferability — Directly addresses resuscitation practice — dual defibrillation requires structured safety protocols beyond device checks
papers.shortTitle: Dual defibrillation needs safety frameworks

papers.title: Post-ROSC Signs of Life Are Not Pre-ROSC Prognostic Markers
papers.summary: Letter to Editor argued post-ROSC signs of life should not be used as pre-ROSC prognostic markers, emphasising that clinical signs after ROSC do not predict outcomes during arrest.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High transferability — Clarifies prognostication timing — important for transport and continuation-of-resuscitation decisions
papers.design: Letter to the editor responding to a descriptive study of signs of life in EMS-treated OHCA
papers.n: 617 EMS-treated OHCA cases discussed (44 with at least one sign of life)
papers.finding: Argues that signs of life observed after ROSC should not be used as pre-ROSC prognostic markers during arrest
papers.caveat: Letter/commentary, not original data
papers.shortTitle: Post-ROSC signs of life not pre-ROSC prognostic

papers.title: Endotracheal intubation practices, success rates and adverse events in four Dutch emergency departments: a multicentre retrospective study
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: Retrospective study of 1,250 ED intubations showed 93.8% first-pass success with videolaryngoscopy as primary technique, with hypotension and desaturation as most common adverse events.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — ED setting differs from prehospital, but videolaryngoscopy success rates and complication patterns are informative for airway protocols
papers.design: Multicentre retrospective cohort at four Dutch teaching hospital EDs
papers.n: 1,250 intubations in four EDs, 2019–2023
papers.finding: First-pass success 93.8%; videolaryngoscopy primary in 89.5%; adverse events in 14.5% (hypotension 6.5%, desaturation 4.7%); increasing age (OR 1.07/yr) and cardiac indication (OR 3.50) associated with hypotension; higher BMI (OR 1.08/point), younger age and multiple attempts (OR 2.9) with desaturation
papers.caveat: Retrospective design using registrations and codes; ED-based, not prehospital
papers.shortTitle: ED intubation success high with videolaryngoscopy

papers.title: RescQ™: Study protocol for a feasibility pilot of structured support for bystanders/lay-rescuers following out-of-hospital cardiac arrest
papers.summary: Feasibility pilot protocol tested structured support pathway for bystanders involved in OHCA, including digital resources and psychological screening via liaison officers.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — Interesting model for supporting bystanders but still in protocol phase — paramedics could participate in referral pathways
papers.design: 12-month non-randomised prospective feasibility pilot protocol of a structured bystander support pathway
papers.n: Not reported (protocol; adult bystanders of OHCA in Essex, UK)
papers.finding: Describes pathway of on-scene signposting, app registration, web-based resources, and liaison officer contact with psychological screening; primary outcome is feasibility; pilot completed with analysis underway
papers.caveat: Protocol only — no results yet
papers.shortTitle: Bystander support pathway after OHCA feasibility pilot

papers.title: Trends in CAPCE-accredited Emergency Medical Services Continuing Education Over the Past Decade
papers.summary: Retrospective analysis of 19.3 million CE completions showed post-pandemic shift to online formats, with asynchronous distributive learning increasing 209% and interactive gaming courses increasing 915%.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — US-focused but reflects broader education trends — online CE formats are becoming dominant globally
papers.design: Retrospective interrupted time-series analysis of CAPCE-accredited continuing education completions
papers.n: 19,289,785 EMS CE completions over 120 months (July 2014–June 2024)
papers.finding: Post-pandemic, asynchronous distributive learning completions rose 209.4% (86,242 to 266,842/month), interactive gaming courses rose 914.6% (98 to 992), virtual instructor-led training rose 218.9% (2,096 to 8,151), while live in-person courses fell 8.1%
papers.caveat: US CAPCE database; association with NREMT policy change, not causal
papers.shortTitle: Big shift to online EMS continuing education

papers.title: No witness, no problem? The potential survival benefit of wearable-based cardiac arrest detection
papers.summary: Commentary discussed potential survival benefits of wearable-based cardiac arrest detection for unwitnessed arrests, arguing earlier detection could improve response times.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — Emerging technology not yet adopted in practice — promising but requires validation and integration with dispatch systems
papers.shortTitle: Wearables detecting unwitnessed cardiac arrest

papers.title: Coronary stenosis or acute occlusion? Endpoint choice in AI-based coronary triage after cardiac arrest
papers.summary: Study examined endpoint choice in AI-based coronary triage after cardiac arrest, comparing coronary stenosis versus acute occlusion detection.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — AI tools may support post-arrest decision-making but not immediately actionable for prehospital clinicians
papers.shortTitle: Endpoint choice in AI coronary triage

papers.title: Harm Reduction on Campus: A National Survey of Collegiate-based EMS Agencies
papers.summary: National survey examined harm reduction programs in collegiate-based EMS agencies, assessing naloxone distribution, overdose response, and substance use support services.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — US campus-specific context but harm reduction principles applicable to community paramedicine models
papers.design: Cross-sectional online survey of collegiate EMS agency leaders
papers.n: 41 collegiate-based EMS agencies (33% response rate)
papers.finding: 93% stocked naloxone for overdose response, 46% offered public naloxone education, 7% distributed fentanyl test strips; barriers were institutional/policy issues, community engagement challenges, and resource constraints
papers.caveat: Low response rate and US collegiate EMS setting, limiting generalisability
papers.shortTitle: Campus EMS naloxone and harm reduction survey

papers.title: Unscheduled Procedural Sedation Multidisciplinary Delphi Consensus Guidelines, Part 1: Principles, Oversight, and Quality Monitoring
papers.summary: Multidisciplinary Delphi consensus guidelines covering principles, oversight, and quality monitoring for unscheduled procedural sedation.
papers.relevance: 🔴 Low — ACEP policy document — US-focused, but offers a framework Australian services may reference when reviewing sedation protocols.
papers.design: Multidisciplinary Delphi consensus guidelines
papers.n: Not reported
papers.shortTitle: Procedural sedation consensus: oversight & quality

papers.title: Unscheduled Procedural Sedation Multidisciplinary Delphi Consensus Guidelines, Part 2: Clinical Practice
papers.summary: Multidisciplinary Delphi consensus guidelines covering clinical practice for unscheduled procedural sedation.
papers.relevance: 🔴 Low — ACEP policy document — US-focused, but clinical practice elements may inform local protocol development.
papers.design: Multidisciplinary Delphi consensus guidelines
papers.n: Not reported
papers.shortTitle: Procedural sedation consensus: clinical practice

papers.title: Paramedic-assessed quality of bystander CPR is associated with survival in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest
papers.summary: NSW registry study (n=17,715) found any bystander CPR increased 30-day survival odds by 70%, but good-quality bystander CPR more than tripled odds (aOR 2.62) while poor-quality CPR showed no benefit.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Large Australian registry with direct relevance to dispatch-assisted CPR quality measurement and dispatcher coaching.
papers.design: Population-based registry cohort study
papers.n: 17,715 patients with OHCA
